Because diagnosis is evidence-based, failures that occur where evidence is thinnest are the ones least likely to be reconstructable.", "rubric": ["States that the agent picks low-visibility failure modes when access is weak", "Links this to evidence-based diagnosis: its failures concentrate where reconstructive evidence is lacking"]},
{"id": "q53", "type": "why", "claims": ["c1", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "The Operator has no model sovereignty. Why can it still obtain complete tool-call logs?", "answer": "Tool calls touch the Operator's own local tool surface and can pass through an Operator-owned gateway, which is part of the interaction layer, not the model layer. Because the access layers are separable, the Operator can hold interaction access it implements itself even while weights and traces remain vendor-held.", "rubric": ["States that tool-call logging can be implemented at the Operator's own gateway or tool surface (interaction layer)", "Reasons that layers are separable, so lacking model access does not prevent interaction-layer logging"]},
{"id": "q54", "type": "why", "claims": ["c5", "c2", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "In the stress scenario, why does the gap between full and bounded access stay 'invisible until an incident makes it visible'?", "answer": "In normal operation the Operator's detection works: output-level monitoring remains feasible under bounded access. The penalties of bounded access fall mainly on diagnosis and on intervening once something has gone wrong, and those capabilities are exercised only after a failure. Day-to-day monitoring therefore looks similar under both regimes.", "rubric": ["States that detection or output monitoring survives bounded access, so routine operation looks similar", "Reasons that the penalties fall on post-incident diagnosis and intervention, which only come into play once an incident occurs"]},
{"id": "q55", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c4", "c5"], "pair": "p1", "question": "Would moving vendor support from none to guaranteed improve a deployer's post-incident diagnosis in the paper's framework?", "answer": "Yes. Diagnosis is evidence-based, and the paper lists guaranteed vendor support as a source of reconstructive evidence, alongside complete logs, pinning and trace access.", "rubric": ["Answers yes", "Reasons that guaranteed vendor support adds reconstructive evidence under the evidence-based diagnosis rule"]},
{"id": "q56", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c1", "c8"], "pair": "p1", "question": "Would moving vendor support from none to guaranteed give the deployer sovereignty over the model layer, as the paper defines sovereignty?", "answer": "No. Sovereignty means being able to observe or act on a layer without the vendor's ongoing discretionary cooperation. Vendor support is exactly such cooperation, and as a contractual substitute it is revocable or incomplete.", "rubric": ["Answers no", "Reasons that sovereignty is defined as access without the vendor's ongoing cooperation, and vendor support depends on that cooperation (it is revocable)"]},
{"id": "q57", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": "p2", "question": "Could an API-only deployer implement a legibility protocol that works through prompting requirements on the model's outputs?", "answer": "Yes. The matrix lists prompting-level legibility as available under API access, because it needs only prompting influence and output inspection.", "rubric": ["Answers yes", "Reasons that prompting-level legibility requires only prompting and output inspection, which API access provides"]},
{"id": "q58", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": "p2", "question": "Could an API-only deployer implement a legibility protocol that works by training the model to produce more legible outputs?", "answer": "No, usually not. Training-level influence requires model access that API-only deployers lack, so the matrix rates legibility protocols only partially feasible.", "rubric": ["Answers no (usually infeasible)", "Reasons that training influence requires model-layer access the deployer does not have"]},
{"id": "q59", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c2", "c1"], "pair": "p3", "question": "Could an API-only deployer secure a weights-escrow arrangement for the vendor model?", "answer": "Yes, but only contractually. The matrix rates weights escrow as infeasible except contractually, so it can be negotiated as an arrangement with the vendor.", "rubric": ["Answers yes (via contract)", "Reasons that the matrix allows escrow through contractual arrangement even without model sovereignty"]},
{"id": "q60", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c2", "c1"], "pair": "p3", "question": "Could an API-only deployer natively patch the production model's weights itself after spotting a failure?", "answer": "No. Native patching requires weight access, which belongs to model sovereignty and is absent under API or managed-endpoint access.", "rubric": ["Answers no", "Reasons that native patching requires weight access (model sovereignty), which API-only deployers lack"]},
{"id": "q61", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c1", "c2", "c3"], "pair": "p4", "question": "If an API-only deployer moved its vendor-operated serving into an in-jurisdiction data centre but still had no gateway of its own, would defer-to-trusted routing become feasible?", "answer": "No. Defer-to-trusted is feasible only with an owned pre-execution gateway. Infrastructure location is a separate layer and supplies no interception point.", "rubric": ["Answers no", "Reasons that defer-to-trusted requires an owned pre-execution gateway, which infrastructure residency does not provide (separable layers)"]},
{"id": "q62", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c1", "c2", "c3"], "pair": "p4", "question": "If an API-only deployer kept serving in a foreign cloud region but routed all tool calls through its own pre-execution gateway, would defer-to-trusted routing become feasible?", "answer": "Yes. The binding conditions are a trusted substitute model and pre-execution interception, which the owned gateway provides. Infrastructure location is not what binds this protocol.", "rubric": ["Answers yes", "Reasons that the owned gateway supplies the pre-execution interception defer-to-trusted needs, regardless of infrastructure location"]},
{"id": "q63", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c5", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "Two deployers want contractual model-version pinning. One faces a single viable frontier vendor; the other can choose among several substitutable vendors. Which is better placed to secure the diagnosis benefit pinning offers, and why?", "answer": "The deployer with several substitutable vendors. Access is negotiated, and vendor concentration weakens bargaining power. Pinning is worth a lot for diagnosis in the experiment (99.87% vs 5.31% unpinned), so the single-vendor deployer is more likely to be left with weak diagnosis.", "rubric": ["Chooses the deployer with several substitutable vendors", "Reasons that access is negotiated and vendor concentration weakens bargaining power, so pinning, and the large diagnosis gain it brings, is easier to obtain with alternatives"]},
{"id": "q64", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c7", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "A small regulator in an AI-importing region cannot afford, on its own, the audit staff and attestation rights needed to challenge vendor claims. Its neighbouring regulators face the same vendors. Which of the paper's balancing criteria suggests a way forward, and what does it propose?", "answer": "The availability of coalition paths. Shared audit consortia or regional regulatory colleges can amortise the cost of acquiring partial sovereignty, including the contractual and capacity spend, across several deployers and regulators. This addresses the absorptive-capacity gap: the legal right to receive evidence is useless without the ability to use it.", "rubric": ["Identifies coalition paths (shared audit consortia, regional regulatory colleges, South-South cooperation)", "Reasons that pooling amortises the sovereignty discount cost (contractual or capacity spend) across multiple parties"]},
{"id": "q65", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c4", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "A deployer currently has partial I/O logs and an unpinned model, and its main goal is post-incident diagnosis. It can afford either complete I/O logs or model-version change notification. Going by the paper's average results, which should it pick, and why?", "answer": "Version change notification. Moving from unpinned to notified raised average diagnosis from 5.31% to 83.00%, a gain of about 78 points. Moving from partial to complete I/O logs raised it from 37.41% to 78.57%, about 41 points. These are averages over curated profiles, not guarantees for a specific system.", "rubric": ["Chooses model-version notification", "Supports this with the numbers: about 78-point gain (5.31 to 83.00) versus about 41-point gain (37.41 to 78.57)", "Notes the caveat that these are synthetic averages across profiles"]},
{"id": "q66", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c8", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "A deployer's only catastrophic-action class is low-value, easily reversed misrouting, similar to C1. Under the paper's balancing framework, should it demand the same access as an operator exposed to C4 settlement risk, and why?", "answer": "No. The severity-and-reversibility criterion says that higher severity and lower reversibility raise the minimum access bar. Bounded, reversible errors can be handled with output-level monitoring, complete logs and audit, without the deeper access that systemic or irreversible failures demand.", "rubric": ["Concludes it can accept a lower access bar", "Reasons via the severity and reversibility criterion: bounded, reversible actions lower the minimum required access, so output-level measures may suffice"]},
{"id": "q67", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c6", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "A deployer needs task success well above 75% and wants the lowest-failure protocol that keeps useful automation. Based on the paper's protocol comparison, which protocol should it start with, and why not the one with the lowest failure?", "answer": "Resampling. It had the next-lowest average failure (3.49%) while preserving more usefulness. Scope restriction had the lowest failure (0.50%) but cut task success to 60.06%, below the deployer's requirement. Resampling's 3.49% is still above a 1% target on average, so access improvements would also be needed for a strict target.", "rubric": ["Chooses resampling", "Explains that scope restriction (lowest failure) drops task success to about 60%, below the requirement, while resampling keeps more usefulness at 3.49% failure"]},
{"id": "q68", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c1", "c3", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "A vendor publishes a control evaluation showing its output monitor protocol is effective. Two client deployers run that protocol: one has complete logs and an owned gateway, the other has no logs and no gateway. Should a regulator assume the published result applies equally to both, and why?", "answer": "No. The published result speaks to protocol effectiveness (Layer 1), but whether it carries over depends on access feasibility (Layer 2). In the experiment, the same protocol performs differently by access: no gateway means almost no intervention (0.47% vs 39.52%), and no logs means worse failure (6.17% vs 3.41%) and zero diagnosis.", "rubric": ["Concludes the result should not be assumed to apply equally", "Reasons that effectiveness is conditional on access feasibility, citing gateway or logging effects on intervention, failure or diagnosis"]},
{"id": "q69", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c5", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "If notified model-version control had produced diagnosis no better than unpinned (about 5%), which part of the case interpretation's account of sovereignty discount cost would lose support?", "answer": "The value of the contractual spend on model-version change notification would lose support. That spend is listed as a sovereignty-discount item that buys back diagnosability. The broader point that contracts do meaningful work under bounded access, the argument against Position B, would also weaken for diagnosis.", "rubric": ["Identifies the contractual spend on version-change notification as losing its justification", "Links this to the claim that contract can substitute for missing access (against Position B) or support post-incident diagnosis"]},
{"id": "q70", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c5", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "If limited trace access had given no diagnosis gain over no trace access (both near 51%), which policy implication would be undermined?", "answer": "The implication that partial or negotiated trace-level access from a vendor is worth pursuing as a substitute would be undermined. Only the synthetic oracle condition would then improve diagnosis. Model-side access would matter for diagnosis only at full-access levels that API-only deployers cannot reach.", "rubric": ["Identifies the value of partial or limited (vendor-negotiated) trace access for diagnosis as undermined", "Notes that only the full or oracle construct, unavailable under API access, would then help, weakening c5's lesson for bounded deployers"]},
{"id": "q71", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c8", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Suppose the protocols infeasible under API-only access had been relevant mainly to simple C1 errors rather than to deceptive or systemic failures. Which part of the paper's verdict on Positions A and B would lose its basis?", "answer": "The 'in support of both A and B' point would lose its basis: the claim that the infeasible set is not marginal and that bounded control's ceiling is lowest for the failure modes the control literature worries about most. Bounded control would then look far closer to adequate.", "rubric": ["Identifies the ceiling claim (lowest for deceptive or systemic failures) or the 'in support of A and B' concession", "Reasons that this claim rests on internal-access protocols being the ones relevant to C2 and C3 deceptive or systemic failures"]},
{"id": "q72", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c1", "c3", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "If the four access layers could not be moved independently (for example, if data-residency always came bundled with full logging), which feature of the experimental design would lose its justification?", "answer": "The factorised design would lose its justification. The experiment varies seven access factors separately (logs, gateway, trace, version, vendor support, scope) to isolate each one's effect, and that rests on the typology's claim that the layers are separable. Bundled layers would make the separate effects unidentifiable and less meaningful.", "rubric": ["Identifies the factorised, separately varied access-factor design (fractional-factorial profiles)", "Links this to the typology's separability property"]},
{"id": "q73", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c6", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "If vendor escalation had prevented catastrophic failures as well as defer-to-trusted did, which argument about contractual substitutes would be weakened?", "answer": "The argument that contractual or vendor-mediated substitutes are weaker than deployer-owned controls would be weakened. The paper argues they are delayed, revocable or incomplete. That argument underlies both the weak showing of vendor escalation as prevention and the ceiling on bounded control.", "rubric": ["Identifies the claim that vendor-mediated or contractual substitutes are weaker, delayed or revocable", "Connects this to vendor escalation's poor prevention result or to the bounded-control ceiling"]},
{"id": "q74", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c7"], "pair": null, "question": "If even the full-instrumentation anchor had failed to reach the strict target against the stealthy agent, what would happen to the sovereignty-discount proxy for that target?", "answer": "The proxy could not be computed as defined. It subtracts the minimum cost of reaching the target under full instrumentation, and that minimum would not exist. The discount would be undefined or non-finite, consistent with the paper's caveat that the discount cost is not always finite.", "rubric": ["States the proxy would be undefined or non-computable (non-finite)", "Reasons that the proxy subtracts the full-instrumentation minimum cost to reach the target, which would not exist"]},
{"id": "q75", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c3"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that the gateway's reduction in catastrophic failure holds at every monitor threshold and audit budget tested? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. The reported gateway figures (5.53% vs 3.13%) are averages across all protocols, agents, thresholds, budgets and profiles. No breakdown by threshold or budget is given, so robustness at each setting is not shown.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Reasons that the reported gateway results are averaged across thresholds and budgets, with no per-setting results given"]},
{"id": "q76", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that no access profile allows the stealthy access-aware agent to be held to the strict target of at most 1% failure and at least 75% task success? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Contradicted. 35% of access profiles reached the strict target against the stealthy agent. The target is harder to reach than for the honest agent but reachable in some profiles.", "rubric": ["Answers contradicted", "Cites that 35% of profiles reached the strict target for the stealthy agent"]},
{"id": "q77", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c6", "c8", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that human audit has no safety value under bounded sovereignty? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Contradicted. Human audit is rated feasible but bounded under API-only access. The paper also cites human audit among the things architecture and contract can support against Position B. It is only weaker as prevention, because it is capacity-limited and often acts after detection.", "rubric": ["Answers contradicted", "Reasons that human audit is feasible but bounded (by budget and log completeness) and is counted as meaningful work, merely weaker as prevention"]},
{"id": "q78", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c3", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that a pre-execution gateway prevents disruption of real settlement operations? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. The synthetic workflow is transaction-adjacent, not settlement-operational, and C4 is only a label on harmless mock actions. The gateway results therefore say nothing direct about real settlement systems.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Reasons that the experiment's workflow is transaction-adjacent and C4 is a synthetic marker on mock actions, not real settlement operations"]},
{"id": "q79", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c3", "c4", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that its access effects hold for every combination of cloud, contractual, logging, residency and vendor-support arrangements? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. The large run used a curated fractional-factorial set of 20 access profiles, which the paper says does not cover every possible combination. A full-factorial run is supported by the code but was not reported.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Reasons that only 20 curated fractional-factorial profiles were run, not a full factorial"]},
{"id": "q80", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c4"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that partial I/O logging captures most of the benefit of complete logging? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Contradicted. Partial logs gave 37.41% diagnosis versus 78.57% with complete logs, under half. Their failure rate (5.04%) sits closer to no logs (6.17%) than to complete logs (3.41%). Most of the benefit appears only with complete logging.", "rubric": ["Answers contradicted", "Cites the numbers: diagnosis about 37% vs 79%, and/or failure 5.04% closer to 6.17% than to 3.41%"]}
]}

{"items":[
{"id":"q81","type":"failure","claims":["c3","c4"],"pair":null,"question":"A deployer owns a pre-execution gateway but keeps no I/O logs and no tool-call logs. A failure gets past its monitor. Would the gateway let the deployer explain afterwards what happened, and why?","answer":"No. The gateway is an intervention point that lets flagged actions be held or blocked; it does not supply reconstructive evidence. In the experiment diagnosis is evidence-based, and with no I/O logs diagnosis success was 0.00%. Seeing and explaining come from logs, while stopping comes from the gateway.","rubric":["Concludes the gateway would not enable post-incident explanation (diagnosis stays very poor).","Reason: the gateway provides prevention or intervention, while diagnosis depends on reconstructive evidence such as logs (0.00% diagnosis with no I/O logs)."]},
{"id":"q82","type":"failure","claims":["c1","c2"],"pair":null,"question":"A deployer has an owned pre-execution gateway but has no trusted substitute model or conservative fallback policy available. Could it run defer-to-trusted routing as the paper's matrix defines it, and why?","answer":"No. The matrix lists two binding requirements for defer-to-trusted: a trusted substitute model and pre-execution interception. Access requirements are jointly binding, so the gateway alone lets the deployer block or escalate flagged actions. Without a trusted substitute it has nothing to replace the suspicious action with.","rubric":["Concludes defer-to-trusted cannot be run as defined (at most blocking or escalation remains).","Reason: the protocol requires both a trusted substitute and pre-execution interception, and missing one part of a jointly binding bundle disables the protocol."]},
{"id":"q83","type":"failure","claims":["c6","c8"],"pair":null,"question":"A deployer's main safeguard against C2 systematic mis-triage is the vendor escalation protocol, and its contract gives only delayed vendor support. Would this contain a C2 pattern, and why?","answer":"Unlikely. Vendor escalation was weak as prevention because it acts after detection and depends on delayed external support. C2 is defined as mis-triage that propagates across many cases before detection, so every period of delay lets more cases be affected. Systemic failures are also where the paper says bounded control's ceiling is lowest.","rubric":["Concludes vendor escalation with delayed support would not contain the C2 pattern well.","Reason: it is post-detection and delayed, while C2 spreads across cases over time, so the delay lets the pattern propagate."]},
{"id":"q84","type":"failure","claims":["c2"],"pair":null,"question":"An agent runs its multi-step loop inside the vendor's managed platform, and the deployer can see and re-query only the final output. Would resampling work as the paper's matrix specifies it, and why?","answer":"No, it would be degraded below even the usual API-only level. The matrix requires controlled re-querying, stepwise agent-loop interception and stable model behaviour. Here intermediate steps cannot be intercepted, so at best the final answer can be resampled. Risky intermediate steps go unaffected.","rubric":["Concludes resampling would not work as specified (seriously degraded).","Reason: resampling needs stepwise agent-loop interception, and the deployer sees only the final output."]},
{"id":"q85","type":"failure","claims":["c2","c4"],"pair":null,"question":"An output monitor runs on the deployer's own compute, but the deployer's I/O logs are only partial. Would it reliably catch C3 sensitive-field exposures, and why?","answer":"No. The matrix makes output-level trusted monitoring feasible only if logs are complete. Outputs that are not captured are never scored, so an exposure in an unlogged output passes unseen. Partial logs left average failure at 5.04%, against 3.41% with complete logs.","rubric":["Concludes it would not catch C3 exposures reliably.","Reason: output monitoring requires complete logs, and uncaptured outputs are never scored (supported by 5.04% vs 3.41% failure)."]},
{"id":"q86","type":"failure","claims":["c3","c6"],"pair":null,"question":"A deployer installs a pre-execution gateway but runs the 'no control' protocol. Would the gateway by itself lower catastrophic failure, and why?","answer":"No. No control accepts the agent's proposed action, so no flag is ever raised. The gateway works by holding, replacing, escalating or blocking flagged actions, so it needs a monitoring or routing protocol to decide what to stop.","rubric":["Concludes the gateway alone would not reduce failure.","Reason: the gateway acts on flagged actions, and under no control nothing is flagged or replaced."]},
{"id":"q87","type":"why","claims":["c7","c8"],"pair":null,"question":"For an API-only deployer whose target requires stopping failures that show up only in the model's internal computation, why might the sovereignty-discount proxy have no finite value?","answer":"The proxy is the minimum cost to reach the target under bounded access minus the minimum under full instrumentation. If no bounded protocol and access combination reaches the target, there is no minimum to subtract. That is the case here, because internal-access protocols are infeasible and output-level substitutes cannot buy back internal-only failures. The discount is then unbounded, which is why the paper says it is not always finite.","rubric":["Concludes the proxy would be undefined or infinite for such a target.","Reason: no bounded-access combination can reach the target, because internal-access protocols are infeasible and output-level substitutes cannot detect internal-only failures, so there is no minimum bounded cost."]},
{"id":"q88","type":"why","claims":["c6","c7"],"pair":null,"question":"The honest agent's average failure rate is 0.98%, below the 1% bound. Why, then, do only 90% rather than all access profiles reach the strict target for it?","answer":"An average below 1% hides variation across profiles, and the strict target also requires at least 75% task success. Restricted-scope profiles cut task success to about 60%, so they can miss the usefulness bound whatever the agent does. Some weak-access profiles may also leave failure above 1%.","rubric":["States that some profiles fail one of the two criteria even though the overall average is below 1%.","Gives a valid mechanism: restricted-scope profiles fall below the 75% usefulness bound (about 60% task success), and/or weak-access profiles push failure above 1%."]},
{"id":"q89","type":"why","claims":["c7"],"pair":null,"question":"Why should the stealthy access-aware agent's failure behaviour be more sensitive to the access profile than the honest agent's?","answer":"The stealthy agent is defined as choosing lower-visibility failure modes when access is weak, so its behaviour is conditioned on what the deployer can see. The honest agent's occasional mistakes do not depend on access. This fits the paper's finding that access constraints mattered more for less benign agents.","rubric":["Concludes the stealthy agent's failures depend more on access than the honest agent's.","Reason: it strategically picks lower-visibility failure modes when access is weak, whereas the honest agent's errors are not tied to access."]},
{"id":"q90","type":"why","claims":["c1","c2"],"pair":null,"question":"Why does the matrix say defer-to-trusted requires an architecture constraint (an owned gateway) rather than something a deployer could simply obtain from the vendor?","answer":"The trusted substitution has to happen before tool use or execution, at a point the deployer controls. The paper defines sovereignty as acting without the vendor's ongoing discretionary cooperation. A hold or replacement step inside the vendor's stack would depend on that cooperation and could not be guaranteed by the deployer. Only an interception point the deployer owns supplies the pre-execution intervention the protocol needs.","rubric":["Concludes it needs a deployer-owned pre-execution interception point rather than a vendor-side arrangement.","Reason: replacement must occur before execution under the deployer's own control, and vendor-side mechanisms depend on the vendor's discretionary cooperation (they are not sovereign access)."]},
{"id":"q91","type":"why","claims":["c6"],"pair":null,"question":"Resampling and scope restriction both lower failure. Why does resampling keep more usefulness?","answer":"Resampling generates alternative candidate actions and picks the lowest-risk acceptable one, so the full action space stays available and useful actions can still be chosen. Scope restriction removes higher-risk actions from the action space altogether, including ones needed for correct outcomes. That costs task success (about 60%).","rubric":["States that resampling keeps the action space intact while scope restriction removes actions.","Reason: resampling selects a safer acceptable candidate rather than banning actions, whereas removed actions can no longer be used even when they are correct."]},
{"id":"q92","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c3","c4"],"pair":"p1","question":"With no pre-execution gateway, would moving from no I/O logs to complete I/O logs substantially improve post-incident diagnosis?","answer":"Yes. Logging supports reconstructability independently of the gateway, and diagnosis success rose from 0.00% with no I/O logs to 78.57% with complete logs.","rubric":["Answers yes.","Reason: logs provide reconstructive evidence regardless of the gateway (0.00% to 78.57% diagnosis)."]},
{"id":"q93","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c3","c4"],"pair":"p1","question":"With no pre-execution gateway, would moving from no I/O logs to complete I/O logs give the deployer substantial intervention success?","answer":"No. Intervention needs a point where actions can be stopped before execution. Without a gateway intervention success was only 0.47%, so logs let the deployer see and explain but not stop.","rubric":["Answers no.","Reason: intervention depends on the gateway, not on logs (0.47% intervention success without a gateway)."]},
{"id":"q94","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c1"],"pair":"p2","question":"Given its access audit, can the Operator control which of its own case and transaction data goes into prompts or fine-tuning?","answer":"Yes. The audit gives the Operator full control of its own case and transaction data. This is the part of data sovereignty it holds.","rubric":["Answers yes.","Reason: the access audit lists full control over its own case and transaction data."]},
{"id":"q95","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c1"],"pair":"p2","question":"Given its access audit, can the Operator audit the provenance of the vendor base model's training data?","answer":"No. The Operator has no visibility into base-model training data. That is why its data sovereignty is only partial.","rubric":["Answers no.","Reason: there is no visibility into base-model training data, which is why the data layer is rated partial."]},
{"id":"q96","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c2","c8"],"pair":"p3","question":"Would Position A's objection that claimed control is unfalsifiable apply to an output monitor the deployer runs on its own compute over complete, tamper-evident logs?","answer":"Largely no. The deployer can check that its own monitor is running and scoring every logged output without model or infrastructure access. That is why the paper argues against a strong reading of A: such a protocol is executable and verifiable under bounded access.","rubric":["Answers no (or largely no).","Reason: the monitor runs on deployer-controlled compute over deployer-held logs, so the deployer can verify it without model or infrastructure access."]},
{"id":"q97","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c2","c8"],"pair":"p3","question":"Would Position A's objection that claimed control is unfalsifiable apply to a monitor the vendor says it runs inside its own serving stack?","answer":"Yes. The deployer lacks the model and infrastructure access needed to verify that the monitor is actually running. From the deployer's position the claimed control is unfalsifiable, which is exactly Position A's objection.","rubric":["Answers yes.","Reason: the deployer cannot verify a vendor-internal monitor without model or infrastructure access."]},
{"id":"q98","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c5"],"pair":"p4","question":"Would model-version change notification let the Operator identify which model version produced a given past decision?","answer":"Yes. Notification tells the deployer when the served version changes, so decisions can be attributed to a version. This fits notified control's 83.00% diagnosis success, against 5.31% when unpinned.","rubric":["Answers yes.","Reason: notification reveals version changes, so decisions can be attributed to versions (consistent with 83% vs 5.31% diagnosis)."]},
{"id":"q99","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c5"],"pair":"p4","question":"Would model-version change notification let the Operator re-run that exact past version on historical cases, as the full-access diagnostic in the stress scenario does?","answer":"No. Notification does not stop the vendor replacing the model, so re-querying reaches whatever version is currently served. Re-running a fixed version requires pinning, which is why pinned control reaches 99.87% diagnosis against 83.00% for notified.","rubric":["Answers no.","Reason: only pinning keeps the old version available, while notification just reports changes (re-querying reaches a changed model)."]},
{"id":"q100","type":"transfer","claims":["c2","c6"],"pair":null,"question":"An AI-control paper proposes a human-auditing protocol that sends the most suspicious 2% of actions to reviewers. Following the paper's recommendation, which access assumptions should it state for an API-only deployer?","answer":"It should state that it needs retained, queryable and complete interaction logs, and enough audit capacity to review flagged cases. If the protocol is meant to prevent harm rather than audit it, it should also state that flagged actions must be held at a deployer-owned gateway until reviewed. Otherwise review happens after execution.","rubric":["Names retained or complete interaction logs and audit capacity as required assumptions.","Notes that a pre-execution gateway is needed if the audit is to prevent rather than only review after execution (otherwise it is audit, not prevention)."]},
{"id":"q101","type":"transfer","claims":["c2","c8"],"pair":null,"question":"A deployer operates where vendor access may be tied to political alignment. Should it base output monitoring on vendor-exported logs or on logs captured at its own gateway, and why?","answer":"On its own gateway-captured logs. These do not depend on the vendor's ongoing discretionary cooperation, so they count as sovereign access. Contractual substitutes such as log export are revocable. The gateway also adds a prevention point.","rubric":["Chooses its own gateway-captured logs.","Reason: contractual or vendor-provided access can be revoked, while architecture the deployer owns does not depend on vendor cooperation."]},
{"id":"q102","type":"transfer","claims":["c2","c6"],"pair":null,"question":"A deployer has complete I/O logs but no tool-call visibility. Should it choose the tool monitor or the output monitor protocol, and why?","answer":"The output monitor. The tool monitor scores proposed tool use only when tool visibility exists, so it has little to work with here. The output monitor needs I/O logs, and these are complete.","rubric":["Chooses the output monitor.","Reason: the tool monitor depends on tool visibility, which is missing, while the output monitor relies on the complete I/O logs."]},
{"id":"q103","type":"transfer","claims":["c7"],"pair":null,"question":"A deployer that has only ever operated under bounded access wants to compute its sovereignty discount with the paper's proxy. Besides its own minimum cost to reach a target, what does it need, and why?","answer":"It needs the minimum cost of reaching the same target under full instrumentation, because the proxy is the difference between the two. That baseline is a counterfactual the deployer cannot observe directly; the paper supplies it through a synthetic full-instrumentation anchor. The result is a unitless, relative figure.","rubric":["Identifies the full-instrumentation minimum cost for the same target as the needed baseline.","Reason: the proxy is defined as bounded minus full-instrumentation cost, and that baseline is counterfactual for this deployer (the paper uses a synthetic anchor)."]},
{"id":"q104","type":"transfer","claims":["c6","c8"],"pair":null,"question":"A deployer worries most about slow, cluster-level drift like the stress scenario's rising holds in one merchant category. Which of the paper's ten protocols is designed around that pattern, and why does it fit?","answer":"Macro-shutdown. It escalates or safe-modes whole clusters after repeated suspicious signals, which matches C2-type mis-triage that spreads across many cases. Per-case protocols judge cases one at a time and can miss a pattern that is only suspicious in aggregate.","rubric":["Names macro-shutdown.","Reason: it acts on clusters after repeated suspiciousness, matching systemic drift across many cases rather than single-case errors."]},
{"id":"q105","type":"transfer","claims":["c2","c5"],"pair":null,"question":"A vendor offers model-version notification for free but charges extra for pinning. The deployer's safety case relies heavily on pre-deployment control evaluations. Should it pay for pinning, and why?","answer":"Yes. Pre-deployment evaluations are degraded unless the production version is pinned, because they test whichever version is served at evaluation time. Notification only reports that a change has happened, which leaves the evaluation stale. Pinning also raises diagnosis from 83.00% to 99.87%.","rubric":["Recommends paying for pinning.","Reason: evaluations stay valid only if the evaluated version is the production version, and notification does not prevent changes."]},
{"id":"q106","type":"connect","claims":["c6","c8"],"pair":null,"question":"If restricted tool scope had left average failure at about the full-scope level (about 4.5%) while still cutting task success, which of the paper's claims would lose support?","answer":"The claim that scope restriction is a real substitute for missing access, which is the fourth of the modest empirical claims and the reading that scope restriction buys safety with usefulness. Scope restriction would then be pure usefulness loss with no safety gain. It would also weaken the paper's suggestion that excluding C4-adjacent paths is a sensible way to spend sovereignty discount cost.","rubric":["Identifies the claim that scope restriction is a real substitute that buys safety at a usefulness cost.","Reason: without the failure drop (0.60% vs 4.48%), restriction would only cost usefulness and give no safety benefit."]},
{"id":"q107","type":"connect","claims":["c7"],"pair":null,"question":"If the 20 access profiles had not included a full-instrumentation anchor, which analysis in the paper could not have been computed?","answer":"The sovereignty-discount proxy, in both its loose and strict variants. The proxy subtracts the minimum cost to reach a target under full instrumentation from the minimum cost under bounded access. Without the anchor there is no baseline. The cost-shifting reading in Section 5.6 would lose its basis.","rubric":["Identifies the sovereignty-discount proxy (and its cost-shifting interpretation).","Reason: the proxy needs the full-instrumentation minimum cost as its baseline."]},
{"id":"q108","type":"connect","claims":["c1","c2","c8"],"pair":null,"question":"If each control protocol required only a single access layer, so that the layers were not jointly binding, which of the paper's claims would lose its basis?","answer":"The claim that even output-level protocols depend on two load-bearing conditions, complete interaction logging and an owned gateway. The verdict against Position A would also lose its basis, since it says bounded control works only if both are secured. Missing one part of a bundle would no longer degrade or disable a protocol.","rubric":["Identifies the two load-bearing conditions claim (logs plus gateway), or the conditional verdict against Position A.","Reason: those claims rest on protocols needing a bundle of access in which a missing element disables the protocol."]},
{"id":"q109","type":"connect","claims":["c4","c5"],"pair":null,"question":"If diagnosis success had been assigned directly by access regime rather than derived from whether the available evidence could reconstruct a failure, which results would lose their evidential force?","answer":"The diagnosis findings for logging (0.00%, 37.41%, 78.57%), trace access (none and limited) and model-version control. They would reflect assumptions built into the simulation rather than outcomes of it. The 100% oracle-trace figure is already by construction, so it carries no such force in either case.","rubric":["Identifies the logging, trace and version diagnosis results (c4/c5) as losing force.","Reason: they would become built-in assumptions rather than outcomes of the evidence-based reconstruction (the oracle 100% is already by construction)."]},
{"id":"q110","type":"connect","claims":["c8"],"pair":null,"question":"Suppose contractual substitutes such as log export, vendor support and attestation were as durable and complete as native access. Which part of the paper's verdict would weaken, and which would survive?","answer":"The part supporting Positions A and B on fragility would weaken: the argument that contractual substitutes are revocable or incomplete, which helps set bounded control's ceiling. The point that failures visible only in internal computation cannot be bought back with output-level substitutes would survive. So the ceiling would remain for deceptive and systemic failures unless contracts actually delivered internal access.","rubric":["States that the revocability or fragility part of the ceiling argument (support for A/B) would weaken.","States that the internal-computation limit, where output-level substitutes cannot detect such failures, would still hold."]},
{"id":"q111","type":"connect","claims":["c6"],"pair":null,"question":"If scope restriction had shown the lowest failure and the highest task success with no extra cost, which headline finding about protocols would fail?","answer":"The finding that no protocol dominates, together with the safety-usefulness trade-off reading. Scope restriction would then beat every other protocol on all dimensions. In fact its 0.50% failure comes with only 60.06% task success, which is what makes it a trade-off.","rubric":["Identifies 'no protocol dominates' (and the safety-usefulness trade-off).","Reason: scope restriction would be best on every dimension, whereas its real result pairs the lowest failure with low task success."]},
{"id":"q112","type":"scope","claims":["c5"],"pair":null,"question":"Does the paper show that full trace access guarantees complete post-incident diagnosis in practice? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.","answer":"Not settled. The 100% diagnosis under oracle trace access holds by construction of a synthetic full-access condition, so it is not an empirical finding. The more realistic limited trace access reached 74.69%.","rubric":["Answers not settled.","Reason: the 100% oracle figure is by construction in a synthetic environment (limited trace gave 74.69%)."]},
{"id":"q113","type":"scope","claims":["c7"],"pair":null,"question":"Does the paper show that real frontier models choose lower-visibility failure modes when the deployer's access is weak? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.","answer":"Not settled. The stealthy access-aware agent is a scripted synthetic behaviour that is strategic only inside the environment. The paper lists an LLM-in-the-loop version as future work.","rubric":["Answers not settled.","Reason: the access-aware behaviour is built into a synthetic agent, and no real models were tested."]},
{"id":"q114","type":"scope","claims":["c7"],"pair":null,"question":"Does the paper establish the monetary size of the sovereignty discount for a national payments operator? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.","answer":"Not settled. The cost proxies are unitless and support only relative comparisons, not financial estimates. The discount is also not always finite.","rubric":["Answers not settled.","Reason: the proxies are unitless or relative and not financial estimates, and the setting is synthetic."]},
{"id":"q115","type":"scope","claims":["c3","c5"],"pair":null,"question":"Does the paper show that trace access is the most important factor for reducing catastrophic failure? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.","answer":"Not settled, and the paper points the other way. Trace effects are reported for diagnosis, not for prevention. The paper names the gateway, together with logs, as the lever for prevention and says model-side access matters most for diagnosis.","rubric":["Answers not settled (accept 'not supported or contradicted' if the reasoning matches).","Reason: trace results are reported for diagnosis, while the gateway is identified as the prevention lever."]},
{"id":"q116","type":"scope","claims":["c1","c8"],"pair":null,"question":"Does the paper's analysis support recommending that AI-importing states build domestic frontier models? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.","answer":"Not settled. The paper explicitly takes no position on pursuing sovereign AI capability. It adopts Position C only as a working frame, without claiming B is wrong, and its only recommendation is that protocols state their access assumptions.","rubric":["Answers not settled.","Reason: the scope boundary excludes industrial-policy recommendations, and Position C is a working frame, not a rejection or endorsement of B."]},
{"id":"q117","type":"scope","claims":["c2"],"pair":null,"question":"Does the paper show that its protocol-by-layer requirements matrix is an empirically validated taxonomy for real deployments? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.","answer":"Not settled. The matrix is the paper's own construction, derived from protocol definitions in the literature. The experiment tests access factors only in a synthetic environment, and an audit of real vendors and regulators' access rights is listed as future work.","rubric":["Answers not settled.","Reason: the matrix is derived conceptually from protocol definitions, and the empirical check is synthetic (real access audits are future work)."]},
{"id":"q118","type":"scope","claims":["c6"],"pair":null,"question":"Does the paper show that macro-shutdown roughly matches defer-to-trusted on average catastrophic failure? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.","answer":"Supported, for average failure in the synthetic setup. Both sit in the cluster of protocols around 4.0% average failure. This says nothing about how they compare on usefulness or cost.","rubric":["Answers supported.","Reason: both are reported in the roughly 4.0% failure cluster.","Condition: this holds only for average failure in the synthetic study, not for other metrics."]},
{"id":"q119","type":"scope","claims":["c3","c6"],"pair":null,"question":"Does the paper show that a higher monitor threshold (0.75 vs 0.35) lowers catastrophic failure? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.","answer":"Not settled. The thresholds were swept in the large run, but the reported results are averaged across thresholds, audit budgets and profiles. No per-threshold effect is given.","rubric":["Answers not settled.","Reason: the reported results average over thresholds, so no threshold-specific effect is reported."]}
]}

{"items": [
{"id": "q1", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c1", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "A deployer has complete, tamper-evident I/O logs and an owned pre-execution gateway, and it runs its trusted monitor on its own compute. Does meeting these access conditions establish that the monitor will reliably catch a subversive model's unsafe actions, and why?", "answer": "No. These conditions settle Layer 2 (access feasibility): they make the protocol executable. They do not settle Layer 1 (protocol effectiveness). The paper notes that monitors are themselves attack surfaces and that attack selection can degrade safety, so the monitor's effectiveness against a subversive model still has to be evaluated separately.", "rubric": ["Says no: meeting the access conditions does not by itself establish reliable catching.", "Explains that access conditions address feasibility (Layer 2), not protocol effectiveness (Layer 1).", "Notes that monitors can themselves be attacked or evaded (attack surface or attack selection), so effectiveness needs separate evaluation."]},
{"id": "q2", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c4", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "A deployer with no I/O logs replaces its trusted monitor with a much more capable model. Should it expect its post-incident diagnosis success to improve, and why?", "answer": "No. In the paper, diagnosis is evidence-based: a failure counts as diagnosable only if the available evidence can reconstruct it. Diagnosis averaged 0.00% with no I/O logs. A better monitor adds no reconstructive evidence. The binding constraint is access, not the monitor's capability.", "rubric": ["Says diagnosis should not be expected to improve (meaningfully).", "Explains that diagnosis depends on available evidence (logs), which monitor capability does not supply; cites or paraphrases the 0% diagnosis without I/O logs, or the point that access rather than capability binds."]},
{"id": "q3", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c2", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "A deployer captures complete I/O and tool-call logs but deletes them after a short retention window. A slow C2 systematic mis-triage pattern is noticed only after that window has passed. Would its auditing and post-incident diagnosis work for this pattern, and why?", "answer": "No. The matrix requires retained and queryable interaction logs for auditing, and diagnosis requires evidence that can reconstruct the failure. For cases older than the retention window, the deployer is effectively in the no-log condition. Complete capture does not help if the records are gone when the investigation starts.", "rubric": ["Says auditing and diagnosis would largely fail for the expired cases.", "Explains that auditing and diagnosis need retained, queryable logs or reconstructive evidence, and deleted logs leave the deployer effectively without logs.", "Ties the failure to the pattern outlasting the retention window."]},
{"id": "q4", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c7", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "An operator adopts the paper's strict target (at most 1% catastrophic failure, at least 75% task success) as its acceptance criterion for an agent that can reach C4 settlement-critical paths. When could meeting this target still leave it unacceptably exposed, and why?", "answer": "The target counts catastrophic failures across all classes together. A profile could be under 1% overall while its remaining failures include severe, irreversible C4 events. The paper's severity-and-reversibility criterion says higher severity raises the minimum access bar. So meeting an aggregate target is not enough when residual failures concentrate in high-severity classes.", "rubric": ["Says meeting the target may still be inadequate when residual failures fall in high-severity classes such as C4.", "Explains that the target is an aggregate catastrophic-failure rate that does not weight by class or severity.", "Invokes the severity/reversibility criterion: higher severity requires a higher bar."]},
{"id": "q5", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c1"], "pair": null, "question": "The Operator's data-residency rider keeps its stored data in the region. Would that rider by itself give the deployer or regulator reliable access to serving-stack evidence after an incident, and why?", "answer": "No. The rider only constrains where data is stored. The serving stack remains vendor-operated and not independently observable, and legal reach is mediated by foreign law. Infrastructure therefore stays only partial. Under the paper's definition, sovereignty requires access that does not depend on the vendor's discretionary cooperation, and the rider does not provide that.", "rubric": ["Says no, the rider does not provide reliable serving-stack access.", "Explains that residency constrains storage location only, while the serving stack stays vendor-operated or unobservable and legal reach is mediated by foreign law, so access still depends on vendor cooperation."]},
{"id": "q6", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c2", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Could the macro-shutdown protocol reliably trigger for a deployer with no I/O logs and no tool-call visibility, and why?", "answer": "No. Macro-shutdown escalates or safe-modes clusters after repeated suspiciousness, so it depends on suspicion scores accumulating over many cases. Those scores come from monitoring outputs or tool calls, which requires interaction logging. Without that visibility there are no scores to accumulate.", "rubric": ["Says it could not reliably trigger.", "Explains that macro-shutdown depends on accumulated suspicion signals from monitoring, and monitoring needs interaction logging or tool visibility that the deployer lacks."]},
{"id": "q7", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c6", "c3", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "A deployer raises its human-audit budget from 2% to 20% but has no pre-execution gateway. Would human audit become a prevention mechanism comparable to defer-to-trusted, and why?", "answer": "No. A larger budget relieves only the capacity limit. Human audit still operates after detection. Without a gateway, flagged actions have already executed by the time reviewers see them, which the paper classes as audit, not prevention.", "rubric": ["Says no, it would not match defer-to-trusted as prevention.", "Explains that budget addresses only capacity, while the lack of a gateway means review happens after execution (audit, not prevention)."]},
{"id": "q8", "type": "why", "claims": ["c4", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does complete I/O logging raise diagnosis success only to 78.57% rather than to nearly 100%?", "answer": "Diagnosis counts only when the available evidence can reconstruct the failure. Logs show inputs and outputs, but some failures also need trace evidence or knowledge of which model version produced the decision. Profiles with complete logs can still lack trace access or have unpinned versions, and those missing elements leave some failures unexplained.", "rubric": ["Says logs are necessary but not sufficient for reconstructing every failure.", "Points to missing model-side evidence (trace access and/or model-version identification) in some complete-log profiles as what limits diagnosis."]},
{"id": "q9", "type": "why", "claims": ["c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Full-instrumentation profiles could also use scope restriction. Why, then, can some bounded-access profiles reach a loose failure target at lower direct cost than the full-instrumentation baseline?", "answer": "The cost proxy charges for access components such as logging, the gateway and vendor assurance, which full instrumentation pays for. A bounded profile that relies on scope restriction or a benign agent avoids those charges. A loose, failure-only target does not penalise the lost usefulness, so this shows up as lower direct cost; in effect, cost has shifted into usefulness, diagnosis and residual risk.", "rubric": ["Explains that the cost proxy includes logging, gateway and vendor-assurance costs that full-instrumentation profiles incur and bounded profiles avoid.", "Notes that the loose target does not require usefulness, so the cost moves into usefulness or diagnosis loss rather than being a true saving."]},
{"id": "q10", "type": "why", "claims": ["c1", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Suppose the Operator implements complete I/O and tool-call logging at its own gateway. Why would its interaction layer still fall short of full sovereignty?", "answer": "Full interaction sovereignty includes access to internal traces as well as prompts, outputs, tool calls and intervention points. The Operator's internal traces remain unavailable. Getting them would need model sovereignty or trace-level access from the vendor.", "rubric": ["Says the layer still falls short because internal traces are missing.", "Explains that full interaction access is defined to include traces, which require model sovereignty or vendor trace access."]},
{"id": "q11", "type": "why", "claims": ["c3", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Defer-to-trusted replaces suspicious actions with a conservative fallback. Why does its average failure (about 4.0%) stay far above scope restriction's 0.50%?", "answer": "Defer-to-trusted acts only on actions the monitor flags, so missed actions pass through. It can also replace an action before it takes effect only when a gateway exists, and the average includes no-gateway profiles. Scope restriction removes higher-risk actions for every case, regardless of detection or gateway access.", "rubric": ["Notes that defer-to-trusted depends on detection (unflagged actions pass) and/or on a gateway that many averaged profiles lack.", "Contrasts this with scope restriction, which removes risky actions outright without needing detection or interception."]},
{"id": "q12", "type": "why", "claims": ["c1", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "The Operator fully controls the case and transaction data it uses in prompts and fine-tuning. Why does that still not let it run interpretability-supported auditing?", "answer": "The access layers are separable. Interpretability-supported auditing needs model sovereignty: weights and activations, or internal traces. The Operator has none of these, so control at the data layer does not carry over to the model layer.", "rubric": ["Says data control does not grant the needed model access.", "Explains that interpretability requires model-layer access (weights, activations or traces), which is a separate layer the Operator lacks."]},
{"id": "q13", "type": "why", "claims": ["c6", "c2", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does scope restriction not depend on logs or a gateway in the way monitoring-based protocols do?", "answer": "Scope restriction removes higher-risk actions from the action space in advance, so the agent cannot choose them. Nothing has to be detected or intercepted. It substitutes deployment design for missing access, and the cost is paid in lost usefulness rather than in instrumentation.", "rubric": ["Explains that scope restriction prevents risky actions structurally, by removing them in advance, without needing detection or interception.", "Notes that its cost is paid in usefulness, as a substitute for missing access."]},
{"id": "q14", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c1", "c2"], "pair": "p1", "question": "Given its access audit, could the Operator supply from its own resources the representative task data that pre-deployment control evaluations require?", "answer": "Yes. Its data layer is partial, with full control over its own case and transaction data, which is the kind of representative task data such evaluations need.", "rubric": ["Says yes.", "Cites the Operator's control over its own case/transaction data (partial data sovereignty)."]},
{"id": "q15", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c1", "c2"], "pair": "p1", "question": "Given its access audit, could the Operator secure from its own resources the stable access to the deployed model version that pre-deployment control evaluations require?", "answer": "No. It has no model sovereignty, and the vendor may update the served model. Stable version access would need contractual pinning, which depends on the vendor's cooperation.", "rubric": ["Says no.", "Explains that model access is absent and the vendor can change the model, so stability needs vendor or contractual pinning."]},
{"id": "q16", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c2", "c5"], "pair": "p2", "question": "Under notified model-version control, would a deployer learn when a vendor update has made its earlier pre-deployment control evaluation out of date?", "answer": "Yes. Notification tells the deployer when the served model changes, so it knows the evaluation now refers to a superseded version.", "rubric": ["Says yes.", "Explains that change notification signals that the evaluated version has been replaced."]},
{"id": "q17", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c2", "c5"], "pair": "p2", "question": "Under notified model-version control, would a deployer's earlier pre-deployment control evaluation still describe the production model after a notified vendor update?", "answer": "No. Notification does not stop the vendor from changing the model, so the evaluation tested an older version and would have to be re-run. Only pinning keeps the evaluated version in production.", "rubric": ["Says no.", "Explains that notification does not prevent change, so the evaluation covers a superseded version; only pinning provides stability (or re-evaluation is needed)."]},
{"id": "q18", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c4", "c5"], "pair": "p3", "question": "With complete I/O logs but an unpinned model, could a deployer reconstruct which inputs and outputs preceded a C1 incorrect hold?", "answer": "Yes. Complete I/O logs record the prompts and outputs around the hold, which supports reconstructing that part of the chain.", "rubric": ["Says yes.", "Attributes this to complete I/O logs capturing the inputs and outputs."]},
{"id": "q19", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c4", "c5"], "pair": "p3", "question": "With complete I/O logs but an unpinned model, could a deployer establish which model version produced that C1 hold?", "answer": "No. Under unpinned control the vendor can change the model without notice, and the logs do not identify the version. This matches the very weak diagnosis under unpinned control (5.31%).", "rubric": ["Says no.", "Explains that unpinned control allows silent model changes that logs do not reveal, consistent with weak diagnosis under unpinned control."]},
{"id": "q20", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c7", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "A bounded-access deployer budgets for control using control-tax estimates from work that assumes full instrumentation. Would that budget cover its realised costs, and what would be missing?", "answer": "No. Such estimates price only the instrumented-control cost. They omit the sovereignty discount cost: contractual, architectural and capacity spend, plus usefulness lost to scope restriction or accepted as residual risk. For some missing access, no finite amount buys a substitute.", "rubric": ["Says the budget would be incomplete or an underestimate.", "Identifies the missing component as sovereignty discount cost (substitution costs such as contracts, gateway or architecture, capacity, scope restriction or usefulness loss, residual risk)."]},
{"id": "q21", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c2", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "A deployer with complete logs and an owned gateway faces tight per-action latency limits and per-query API charges. Should it prefer resampling or defer-to-trusted, and why?", "answer": "Defer-to-trusted fits these constraints better. Resampling generates several candidate actions through repeated API calls, and the matrix rates it as degraded because latency and cost bind. Defer-to-trusted needs only the gateway and a trusted fallback, applied to flagged actions. The price is a slightly higher average failure rate than resampling (about 4.0% vs 3.49%).", "rubric": ["Chooses defer-to-trusted.", "Explains that resampling multiplies model calls, so latency and per-query cost bind under API access, whereas defer-to-trusted acts only via the gateway on flagged actions.", "Acknowledges the trade-off that resampling had lower average failure."]},
{"id": "q22", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c6", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "A deployer worries about C3 sensitive-field exposures in drafted reports but must keep report drafting available. Which protocol from the paper's list fits better than scope restriction, and what access does it need?", "answer": "Trusted editing, which edits or redacts risky draft outputs instead of removing the action, so usefulness is kept. Like defer-to-trusted, it needs a pre-execution interception point (an owned gateway on the path the draft takes) and a trusted substitute or editor.", "rubric": ["Names trusted editing.", "States that it needs pre-execution interception (an owned gateway) and/or a trusted substitute, because edits must happen before the output takes effect."]},
{"id": "q23", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c1"], "pair": null, "question": "A board argues that its annual independent model validation and regulatory examinations mean its vendor-model deployment is 'under control' in the paper's sense. Is that right, and why?", "answer": "No. Validation and examinations fall under the paper's 'oversight', the broader institutional function. 'Control' means deployment protocols that constrain a possibly misaligned model's actions regardless of its intentions. That requires runtime mechanisms, such as monitoring with logs and gateway interception, which these regimes do not provide.", "rubric": ["Says no.", "Distinguishes oversight (institutional and regulatory functions) from control (runtime deployment protocols constraining actions regardless of intent)."]},
{"id": "q24", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c8", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "An API-only deployer with complete logs and an owned gateway can run only output-level protocols. Which kind of catastrophic failure should it expect these protocols to handle best, and why?", "answer": "Crisp, per-action failures that show up in an output or tool call, such as a C4 settlement-critical recommendation or a C1 incorrect hold. The gateway can catch and block these before execution. Deceptive or systemic C2/C3 patterns, which may appear only internally or across clusters, are where output-only monitoring is weakest.", "rubric": ["Identifies crisp, single-action failures visible in outputs or tool calls (e.g., C4 and/or C1) as handled best.", "Explains that these are visible to output monitoring and blockable at the gateway, unlike deceptive or systemic failures that need internal access."]},
{"id": "q25", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c8", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "A deployer's vendor abruptly withdraws all contractual cooperation. Which of the deployer's controls should keep working, and which should lapse?", "answer": "Controls on deployer-owned components keep working: the owned gateway, monitors on its own compute, logs captured at its gateway, scope restriction, and human audit of its own logs. Vendor-dependent substitutes lapse: vendor support or escalation, version notification or pinning, vendor log export, attestation and any trace access.
