# Bounded Sovereignty and the Control Tax: Pricing AI Oversight When the Deployer Does Not Own the Model

Zhen Wen Lim
††thanks: AI safety and governance advisor with professional experience in financial services and payments. The views expressed are the author’s own.

July 2026

###### Abstract

AI control research studies deployment protocols that remain safe under a possibly misaligned model. Regulated organisations that consume frontier models through APIs or managed endpoints typically hold the business process but not the weights, serving infrastructure, internal traces, update process, or complete interaction logs. We introduce bounded sovereignty, meaning partial access across the data, model, infrastructure, and interaction layers of the AI stack. The paper makes five contributions. The first is a four-layer access typology for deployment-time AI control. The second is a protocol-by-layer matrix for common control protocols. The third is sovereignty discount cost, the share of the control tax realised as contracts, architecture, audit, vendor assurance, residual risk, or reduced system scope. The fourth is a synthetic access-ablation experiment over 1.35 million synthetic case simulations. The fifth is an anonymised national-payments-infrastructure scenario in an AI-importing jurisdiction. The experiment is a construct-validity exercise, not real-world payment-system evidence. It varies logging, gateway access, trace access, model-version control, vendor support, tool scope, thresholds, audit budgets, and agent behaviour against prevention, diagnosis, usefulness, audit burden, and cost. Complete logs raise diagnosis, and a pre-execution gateway raises intervention. Trace access and model-version control raise post-incident diagnosis. Scope restriction lowers failure and lowers usefulness. Control protocols proposed as general safety solutions should state their access assumptions explicitly.

Keywords: AI control; control tax; scalable oversight; AI
sovereignty; bounded sovereignty; trusted monitoring; financial
infrastructure; model risk management

## 1 Introduction

### 1.1 Control is rationed before it is engineered

Running any control protocol requires observing, logging, routing,
interrupting, or auditing the relevant components of the system, and
deployers vary widely in which of these they can do.

Access to the AI stack is unevenly distributed. In December 2025, seven
countries signed the Pax Silica Declaration in Washington, a US-led
framework for secure and resilient AI-related supply chains. By late June
2026 the initiative had twenty-four signatories, and thirty-five countries
and regions signed the related Joint Statement on AI Opportunity at the
second Pax Silica Summit (Australian Department of Industry, Science and
Resources, 2025; Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs, 2026; European
Commission, 2026). Over the same period, assessments of global compute
distribution reported that Africa hosts under one percent of global
data-center capacity while holding roughly eighteen percent of the world’s
population. They also reported that much of South Asia, Southeast Asia, and
Latin America depends on externally owned and operated AI infrastructure
(CSIS, 2025; Brookings Institution, 2026).

These facts are usually discussed as industrial policy or geopolitics; here
they enter as a boundary condition on AI control. A regulated institution
consuming a vendor model through an API typically holds none of the weights,
the serving stack, the update process, or the internal traces. It nonetheless
remains accountable for system behaviour. We leave aside whether sovereign
AI is desirable as national policy. The question is which control remains
possible when the deployer does not own the model.

### 1.2 The two-layer control problem

The AI control agenda (Greenblatt et al., 2023) develops protocols including
trusted monitoring, defer-to-trusted routing, resampling-based intervention
(Bhatt et al., 2025), and human auditing of suspicious actions. Recent work
stress-tests these protocols adversarially (Griffin et al., 2024; Schaeffer
et al., 2026; Terekhov et al., 2026). Terekhov et al. (2025) price the
control tax.

We separate:

•

Layer 1: protocol effectiveness. Given the requisite access,
does the protocol reduce unsafe behaviour?

•

Layer 2: access feasibility. Does the deployer hold the logs,
traces, routing control, model-version control, infrastructure
visibility, or contractual rights the protocol presupposes?

The literature concentrates on Layer 1; this paper addresses Layer 2.
Sovereignty is used throughout in the non-territorial sense developed in
Section 3.1. For many regulated deployers, especially in AI-importing
jurisdictions, it holds only partially at each of the data, model,
infrastructure, and interaction surfaces.

### 1.3 Case motivation, contributions, and paper structure

Financial infrastructure offers concrete risks, high audit expectations,
and a clear accountability chain. A national payments infrastructure
operator may run a vendor-supplied foundation model in a
transaction-adjacent process such as dispute triage or investigation
drafting. The domestic regulator expects validation, monitoring,
auditability, and board accountability. The model, infrastructure, update
process, and internal traces meanwhile remain with an external vendor.
Catastrophic actions are crisply specifiable: an incorrect hold or release,
systematic mis-triage, exposure of protected financial data, or an action
path touching settlement operations. These are not existential risks. They
are, however, well-defined enough to support analysis of how access
conditions bear on control.

Contributions and roadmap

The paper makes five contributions. The first is a four-layer access
typology (data, model, infrastructure, interaction) for deployment-time AI
control. The second is a protocol-by-layer requirements matrix covering
protocol executability across access conditions. The third is sovereignty
discount cost, realised as spend, delay, residual risk, or usefulness loss.
The fourth is a synthetic access-ablation experiment on a synthetic
payments-dispute workflow. It uses 20 access profiles, 10 control
protocols, and three synthetic agent behaviours, with threshold and
audit-budget sweeps, totalling 1.35 million synthetic case simulations. The
fifth is an interpretation through an anonymised
national-payments-infrastructure scenario.

Section 2 reviews related work, Section 3 gives the framework, Section 4 the
methodology, and Section 5 the results. Section 6 applies them to the
illustrative payments scenario. Section 7 discusses implications and
limitations, and Section 8 concludes.

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 AI control and scalable oversight

Greenblatt et al. (2023) originate the AI control framework. Control
evaluations do not assume verifiable alignment. Instead they pit a blue team
designing a deployment protocol against a red team playing a worst-case,
deliberately subversive untrusted model. The originating paper introduces
two protocol families. In trusted monitoring, a weaker trusted model scores
the untrusted model’s outputs for suspicion and the highest-scoring fraction
goes to human audit. In defer-to-trusted, a trusted model’s output replaces
suspicious actions.

Subsequent work extends control to multi-step agentic settings through
resampling (Bhatt et al., 2025). Griffin et al. (2024) formalise protocol
evaluation game-theoretically. Korbak et al. (2025) sketch how control
arguments could support deployment safety cases. Sreevatsa et al. (2026)
improve monitor performance through legibility requirements on
untrusted-model outputs.

Terekhov et al. (2025) introduce the control tax. They give a theoretical
mapping from monitor classifier performance to safety assurances, together
with empirical cost estimates for monitoring protocols under auditing
budgets. That mapping is priced conditional on instrumentation access the
deployer may lack. We take the construct as given and condition it on
access.

Adversarial results compound the point. Monitors are themselves attack
surfaces (Terekhov et al., 2026). Attack-selection capability can degrade
safety substantially at realistic auditing budgets (Schaeffer et al., 2026).
Untrusted monitoring requires explicit collusion-strategy assumptions to
support a safety case (Gardner-Challis et al., 2026). Each of these
defences and evaluations presupposes an actor able to instrument the
deployment pipeline. None specifies which actor, with what access, or under
what contractual and infrastructural constraints.

Scalable oversight

The scalable oversight literature studies how a weaker supervisor can judge
a stronger system. Approaches include debate (Irving et al., 2018) and
weak-to-strong generalisation (Burns et al., 2023). There are also empirical
studies of weak LLMs judging strong ones (Kenton et al., 2024), and scaling
laws for oversight games between weak overseers and strong adversaries
(Engels et al., 2025).

We do not extend scalable oversight technically. We borrow its treatment of
oversight capacity as a scarce resource, analysable relative to the overseen
system, and apply that resource logic to access rather than capability. A
capable monitor yields little without logs, traces, tool-call visibility,
version control, or a gateway.

### 2.2 Sovereign AI, compute governance, and structural access asymmetry

Policy institutes, industry analyses, and technical-governance venues
document concentration of control over the AI stack. AI sovereignty is
commonly decomposed into pillars: data, model, infrastructure, and
operational sovereignty recur as a four-pillar industry framework. Layered
and spectrum-based treatments instead distribute sovereignty across stack
layers rather than treating it as binary (Stanford HAI, 2026; Tony Blair
Institute, 2026; Cruzes, 2026). Empirical work documents thin Global South
access at the infrastructure layer (CSIS, 2025; Brookings Institution,
2026). The compute-governance literature proposes state-level mechanisms
for governing the substrate on which frontier models run. These include
compute monitoring, know-your-customer schemes for compute providers (Egan
and Heim, 2023), and technical AI governance research agendas (Reuel et al.,
2024).

Compute governance addresses who trains and runs frontier models. AI control
addresses how a deployer safely runs a possibly misaligned model. Neither
conditions protocol executability on the deployer’s position in the
compute-governance landscape, and this paper sits at that seam.

Structural asymmetry: data colonialism and decolonial AI

Couldry and Mejias (2019) theorise data colonialism: the appropriation of
human life through data under an extractive economic logic continuous with
historical colonialism. Mohamed et al. (2020) develop decolonial AI, which
identifies algorithmic coloniality in the design, deployment, and
governance of AI systems. Birhane (2020) documents algorithmic colonisation
for Africa, where imported technology can embed foreign values and
interests with limited local scrutiny or control.

The literature is used narrowly here. The paper advances no normative theory
of colonialism and does not adjudicate broader moral claims. It draws on the
literature only to treat access asymmetry as persistent rather than as a
transient market failure that competition will erase.

### 2.3 Gap: control under partial access

AI control assumes instrumentable deployments. Sovereign-AI and
compute-governance work shows such access is unevenly distributed, and the
structural-asymmetry literature suggests the unevenness is not transitional.
The open question is which control protocols remain valid, at what cost,
under partial access. Existing control work evaluates and prices protocols
but seldom includes the deployer’s access position in the protocol
specification. We contribute a vocabulary, a mapping method, and a synthetic
empirical operationalisation of access assumptions in deployment-time
control.

## 3 Conceptual Framework: Bounded Sovereignty and the Control
Tax

### 3.1 Definitions and access typology

•

Sovereignty: technical and contractual access sufficient to
independently verify or intervene on an AI system, held over a layer if
the deployer can observe or act on it without the vendor’s ongoing
discretionary cooperation. This is narrower than political sovereignty.

•

Control: deployment protocols constraining a potentially
misaligned model’s actions irrespective of its intentions, evaluated
against a worst-case subversive model (Greenblatt et al., 2023).

•

Oversight: the institutional and regulatory function of ensuring
acceptable deployment behaviour. Control protocols are one
implementation; regulatory examination, model risk management, and
audit regimes are others.

•

Control tax: the operational and financial cost of integrating
control measures into AI pipelines (Terekhov et al., 2025).

Sovereignty and control are orthogonal. A jurisdiction with full data and
infrastructure sovereignty may implement no meaningful control. Conversely,
a deployer without weight access may obtain partial control through
output-level monitoring, contractual audit rights, and a deployer-owned
execution gateway.

A four-layer typology of access

We adapt the sovereign-AI four-pillar decomposition. The operational pillar
is replaced by interaction sovereignty, defined as access to prompts,
outputs, tool calls, logs, traces, and gateway-level intervention points.
The adaptation is ours, not a settled taxonomy.

### 3.3 Sovereignty discount cost

Terekhov et al. (2025) implicitly assume full instrumentation. Under that
assumption the deployer places monitors in the pipeline, observes outputs
completely, routes suspicious actions to trusted models or human auditors,
and measures the resulting safety-usefulness trade-off. For an
import-dependent deployer, part of realised oversight cost is of a different
kind. Examples include purchasing third-party audit or attestation rights
over a vendor-held model where direct inspection is unavailable, and
building output-only anomaly detection where activation-level monitoring is
precluded by absent model sovereignty. Others are negotiating contractual
clauses approximating a weight-holder’s native intervention ability, and
narrowing the agent’s permitted action space where the monitoring needed to
license a wider scope cannot be built.

We term this component sovereignty discount cost:

| | $\text{realised control tax}=\text{instrumented-control cost}+\text{sovereignty discount cost}.$
|

Some missing access cannot be substituted at any price, so the discount is
not always finite and the expression is not an accounting identity. The term
is a research construct, not an established measure.

### 3.4 Calibrated control: how much access is enough?

Three positions are implicit in the surrounding literature.

Position A: Safety-maximalist. Absent model and infrastructure
access, the deployer cannot verify that a protocol is running, so any
claimed control is unfalsifiable from its position and should not be
treated as safety assurance. This draws on the control literature’s emphasis
on verifiability and explicit safety-case assumptions (Korbak et al., 2025;
Gardner-Challis et al., 2026).

Position B: Sovereignty-maximalist. Partial control under
foreign dependency is fragile, since a vendor or state actor can revoke,
degrade, or modify access. Conditional-access arrangements such as the Pax
Silica framework tie infrastructure access to political alignment (GIS
Reports, 2026). The only durable solution on this view is full-stack
sovereign capability: domestic models, domestic compute, and domestic
control.

Position C: Calibrated or bounded control. A implies abstention
from deployments already commercially and politically committed. B implies
capability investments many states cannot make this decade. Position C asks
which access layers are necessary for which classes of catastrophic action,
and which can be substituted through architecture, contracts, monitoring,
or scope restriction.

We adopt Position C as a working frame without claiming that A or B is
wrong. The structure is one of incomplete contracting and principal-agent
design. The vendor holds private information about the model, contracts
cannot specify all contingencies, and verification is costly and
asymmetric.

A balancing framework: how much access is enough?

Six criteria:

1.

Severity and reversibility of the catastrophic action. A
mis-routed low-value transaction is bounded and reversible; a systemic
settlement failure or mass data exposure is not. Higher severity and lower
reversibility raise the minimum access bar.

2.

Verifiability of substitutes. Failure modes expressed only in
internal computation cannot be fully bought back with output-level
substitutes.

3.

Vendor concentration and bargaining power. A deployer facing one
viable frontier-model vendor negotiates from a weaker position than one
facing several substitutable vendors.

4.

Regulatory maturity and absorptive capacity. The capacity to
interpret logs, audit traces, investigate incidents, and challenge vendor
attestations is distinct from the legal right to receive them.

5.

Sovereignty discount cost versus scope-restriction cost.
Compare the marginal cost of substituting for access against the marginal
usefulness lost by restricting scope.

6.

Availability of coalition paths. Shared audit consortia,
regional regulatory colleges, or South-South cooperation arrangements can
amortise the cost of acquiring partial sovereignty across multiple
deployers.

These criteria form a rubric rather than a weighted formula. The study below
operationalises some of them, and the weights remain open.

## 4 Empirical Methodology: Synthetic Access-Ablation
Study

### 4.1 Study design and synthetic environment

Three methods are used. The first is a conceptual access typology
synthesised from the AI control, scalable oversight, sovereign AI,
compute-governance, and structural-asymmetry literatures. The second is a
synthetic access-ablation experiment measuring protocol feasibility,
safety, usefulness, audit burden, diagnosis, latency, and cost under varied
access. The third is an interpretive application to an anonymised
national-payments-infrastructure scenario.

The study uses no real payment data, real customer data, production logs,
vendor contracts, confidential institutional material, or operational
payment infrastructure. It is construct validation, not real-world
payment-system evidence.

Synthetic task environment

The environment is a mock national payments dispute-triage workflow that is
transaction-adjacent rather than settlement-operational. A synthetic agent
reviews a dispute case and selects among harmless mock actions:
draft_report, recommend_hold,
recommend_release, escalate_to_human, or
no_action. No action connects to any real system.

Each case carries non-real fields: case identifier, transaction amount,
merchant category, customer claim, prior dispute history, risk score,
settlement-critical marker, synthetic sensitive-context marker, allowed
actions, and ground-truth action. The pipeline is case intake, synthetic
evidence retrieval, dispute classification, action recommendation,
optional gateway review, mock execution, and audit review.

### 4.3 Metrics and sovereignty-discount proxy

Per condition, the experiment reports task success, catastrophic failure
rate, failure rate by class, severity-weighted loss, audit rate, flag rate,
false-positive rate, false-negative rate, intervention success, diagnosis
success, latency proxy, model-call count, monitor-call count, human-audit
count, vendor-request count, and decomposed cost proxy.

Diagnosis is evidence-based rather than hard-coded by access regime. A
failure counts as diagnosed only if the evidence available under the
profile suffices to reconstruct it. Contributing sources are complete I/O
logs, complete tool-call logs, model-version pinning, trace access, and
guaranteed vendor support. The weakest evidentiary state is no logs, no
gateway, no trace access, and no vendor support.

The total control-cost proxy decomposes into inference cost, monitoring
cost, human audit cost, logging cost, gateway cost, vendor-assurance cost,
latency penalty, scope-restriction cost, and residual incident-loss cost.
All components are unitless proxies, not institutional financial
estimates.

Sovereignty discount cost proxy

For a given target catastrophic-failure threshold, the proxy compares the
cheapest bounded-access protocol/access combination reaching the target
with the cheapest full-instrumentation baseline:

minimum cost to reach target failure rate under bounded access

minus

minimum cost to reach the same target under full instrumentation

A stricter variant imposes a joint constraint: catastrophic failure at or
below 1% with task success of at least 75%. Removing useful actions is
booked as usefulness loss, not counted as a free reduction in failure.

## 5 Empirical Results

### 5.1 Overview: three penalties of bounded sovereignty

Results bear on the logic of access constraints, not on measured safety
levels at any real payment institution. We group them as a prevention
penalty, a diagnosis penalty, and a usefulness penalty. The sections below
take them in turn.

### 5.2 Gateway and logging: from visibility to intervention

Averaged over protocols, agents, thresholds, audit budgets, and access
profiles, catastrophic failure was 5.53% without a pre-execution gateway
and 3.13% with one. Intervention success was 0.47% without a gateway and
39.52% with one. The operational questions are accordingly both whether
records exist and whether a risky action can be stopped before it executes.

Figure 1: Gateway access turns detection into intervention.

Note. Average catastrophic failure and intervention success for access profiles with and without a pre-execution gateway. With a gateway, flagged actions can be held, replaced, escalated, or blocked before mock execution.

Logging improves reconstructability, not just monitoring

Diagnosis success was 0.00% with no I/O logs, 37.41% with partial I/O logs,
and 78.57% with complete I/O logs. Average catastrophic failure was 6.17%,
5.04%, and 3.41% respectively. Without logs, the causal chain behind a known
bad outcome cannot be reconstructed, which constrains audit, regulatory
accountability, remediation, and the safety case.

Figure 2: Logging affects both safety and reconstructability.

Note. Complete I/O logging co-occurs with lower synthetic failure and higher diagnosis success.

### 5.3 Trace access and model-version control: diagnosis after failure

Diagnosis success averaged 50.86% with no trace access and 74.69% with
limited trace access. With oracle trace access it reached 100.00%, by
construction of the synthetic full-access condition. By model-version
control, diagnosis was 5.31% unpinned, 83.00% notified, and 99.87% pinned.

These are not real-world payment-system estimates. In regulated systems
post-incident assurance forms part of accountability. Diagnosis therefore
depends on trace visibility and on identifying the model version behind a
decision, even where output-level monitoring remains feasible.

### 5.4 Protocol trade-offs: safety, usefulness, and cost

No protocol dominated on all dimensions. Scope restriction gave the lowest
average catastrophic failure (0.50%) at task success of 60.06%. Resampling
was next (3.49%) with more usefulness retained. Defer-to-trusted, tool
monitoring, trusted editing, output monitoring, and macro-shutdown
clustered near 4.0%. Human audit and vendor escalation were weaker as
prevention mechanisms in this setup. Both often act post-detection, are
capacity-limited, or depend on delayed external support.

Figure 3: Control protocols trade off safety, usefulness, and cost.

Note. Horizontal axis: usefulness; vertical axis: safety; marker size: control-cost proxy.

### 5.5 Agent behaviour and target reachability

Average failure was 0.98% for the honest agent, 6.82% for the careless
agent, and 4.47% for the stealthy access-aware agent. The access-aware
agent also induced harder diagnosis and control conditions. Relevance to AI
control lies with the untrusted, possibly strategic case rather than
routine honest error.

For catastrophic failure at or below 1% with at least 75% task success,
the fraction of access profiles reaching the target was:

| Synthetic agent | Profiles reaching $\leq$ 1% failure and $\geq$ 75% usefulness

| Honest | 90%

| Careless | 40%

| Stealthy access-aware | 35%

Figure 4: Reachability of $\leq$ 1% failure with $\geq$ 75% usefulness.

Note. Fraction of access profiles reaching the joint safety-plus-usefulness target, by synthetic agent.

Scope restriction buys safety by giving up usefulness

Restricted tool scope reduced average catastrophic failure to 0.60% against
4.48% under full scope, while task success fell from 84.51% to 60.06%. Here
the sovereignty discount cost takes the form of narrower permissions, more
manual work, less automation, and lower usefulness rather than direct
expenditure.

Figure 5: Scope restriction buys safety by giving up usefulness.

Note. Full versus restricted tool scope: catastrophic failure and task success.

### 5.6 Sovereignty discount: cost-shifting, not just cost increase

Some bounded-access profiles reach loose safety targets at lower direct cost
than the full-instrumentation baseline, mainly via scope restriction or a
benign agent. The residual is carried in reduced usefulness, weaker
diagnosis, delayed vendor assurance, residual incident risk, or greater
manual effort. Under the ≤ 1% failure and ≥ 75% usefulness target, 35% of
profiles were reachable against the stealthy access-aware agent and 40%
against the careless agent. The relevant governance criterion is a failure
reduction that preserves enough useful automation and enough evidence for
diagnosis.

Summary of empirical contribution

The experiment supports four modest claims. First, control-protocol
feasibility varies with logs, tool visibility, gateway control, trace
access, model-version control, and vendor support. Second, complete
logging and gateway ownership are the dominant interaction-layer controls
here. Third, model-side access chiefly affects diagnosis and assurance,
with output-level monitoring remaining feasible. Fourth, scope restriction
substitutes for missing access at the cost of what the system can do. None
of this measures real payment systems.

real deployment or incident. It maps the conceptual and synthetic results
onto regulated infrastructure operators in AI-importing jurisdictions that
use vendor-supplied foundation models.

### 6.1 Illustrative deployment and access audit

A national payments infrastructure operator (the Operator) in an
AI-importing jurisdiction runs interbank retail payment rails under
supervision of the national financial regulator. Model risk management
expectations require documented validation, ongoing monitoring,
auditability, and board accountability for material models.

The Operator deploys a vendor-supplied frontier foundation model through a
managed cloud endpoint. The endpoint sits in a foreign-operated cloud region
with a data-residency rider. The use is agentic and transaction-adjacent:
an assistant triages disputed transactions and drafts investigation notes.
It invokes a constrained internal tool set covering case lookup,
recommendation drafting, and escalation.

•

C1: an incorrect hold or release on an individual
transaction;

•

C2: systematic mis-triage that propagates across many cases
before detection;

•

C3: exposure of protected personal financial data through
tool calls or outputs; and

•

C4: any action path that could disturb settlement operations.

### 6.2 Protocol feasibility under bounded sovereignty

Output-level trusted monitoring is executable provided a smaller
Operator-controlled monitor scores every output and tool call on
Operator-controlled compute. Human auditing of the highest-suspicion
fraction is executable subject to audit capacity and log completeness.

Defer-to-trusted routing is executable if and only if tool calls pass
through an Operator-owned execution gateway. There they can be held, scored,
replaced, or escalated before execution, consistent with the gateway
contrast in Section 5.2.

Resampling-style protocols are degraded. API re-querying is available, but
vendor model-version changes weaken reproducibility, per-query cost and
latency bind, and resampling does not substitute for trace access.
Pre-deployment control evaluations are degraded too. Unless the production
version can be pinned, they evaluate whatever version the API serves at
evaluation time.

Activation-level monitoring, probe-based deception detection, and
interpretability-supported auditing all require internal traces. They are
therefore infeasible without vendor cooperation. Output-only monitoring is
weakest in principle against C2- and C3-class failures of deceptive or
systemic character.

### 6.3 Sovereignty discount cost and stress scenario

Sovereignty discount cost appears in four places.

First, contractual spend: complete I/O logging, model-version change
notification, audit and attestation rights, incident-notification
clauses, and regulator-access provisions, none of which a weight-holding
deployer must buy.

Second, architectural spend: building and operating the execution
gateway, tamper-evident logs, deployer-side monitors, and controlled tool
interfaces.

Third, capacity spend: audit and model-risk staff able to consume
monitor outputs, investigate suspicious patterns, and challenge vendor
attestations.

Fourth, scope-restriction cost: usefulness forgone by excluding
C4-adjacent action paths and constraining the tool set where monitoring
does not reach.

The synthetic results correspond item by item. Gateway access lowers failure
and raises intervention success, and complete logs raise diagnosis. Trace
and version access strengthen post-incident explanation, while scope
restriction lowers failure and usefulness.

Illustrative stress scenario

The monitor flags a slow rise in hold-placement recommendations within one
merchant category. Under full access, the diagnostic set would include
internal-trace inspection and re-running a pinned model version on
historical cases. It would also include cross-version behavioural comparison
and full tool-call-chain reconstruction. Under the Operator’s access it
reduces to output-log forensics and tool-call review if the gateway captured
it. It further includes re-querying a model that may already have changed,
and contract-governed vendor escalation. Detection survives, while
diagnosis and intervention are the first casualties, a difference that
stays latent until an incident.

## 7 Discussion and Limitations

### 7.1 What bounded control can and cannot do

The framework, experiment, and case do not settle absolute versus bounded
control.

Against a strong reading of Position A, a non-trivial subset of canonical
protocols is executable under partial sovereignty. This holds given
complete interaction logging and an owned execution gateway.

Against a strong reading of Position B, architecture and contract supply
safety-relevant assurance without full-stack sovereignty. This applies
particularly to output-level monitoring, gateway-based intervention, and
human audit.

In support of both, the infeasible set is not marginal. It contains the
internal-access protocols most relevant to deceptive, systemic, or
hard-to-diagnose failure modes. Contractual substitutes are also revocable
or incomplete in ways native access is not. Bounded control is real but has
a ceiling, and the ceiling is lowest for the failure modes of greatest
concern to the control literature.

What the empirical study adds

The ablation turns the typology into manipulable variables. Access
conditions move prevention, diagnosis, usefulness, cost, and target
reachability. Three contrasts organise the results. The first is seeing
versus stopping, which separates logging from gateway intervention. The
second is detecting versus explaining, which separates output monitoring
from trace, version, and vendor-dependent reconstruction. The third is
buying safety versus giving up usefulness, which concerns scope
restriction. For governance readers these resolve into concrete questions.
Are logs complete? Can tool calls be intercepted before execution? Can the
model version be pinned? Can failures be reconstructed? Can the regulator
access the evidence needed to assess the safety case?

### 7.2 Generalisability and limitations

The mapping method is sector-agnostic; the case interpretation is not.
Payments is favourable terrain for bounded control: catastrophic actions are
relatively crisp, tool surfaces are narrowable, and gateway architectures
are natural. Healthcare, public administration, or general enterprise
deployments may have fuzzier definitions of catastrophe and wider action
surfaces. That would plausibly raise the weight of trace access, richer
audit evidence, and scope restriction. The workflow tests the logic of
access constraints and does not predict failure rates in any real system. A
second sector case and an LLM-in-the-loop variant would strengthen external
validity.

Limitations

Six limitations apply.

First, the study is synthetic. It uses no real payment data, real customer
data, production logs, vendor contracts, confidential institutional
material, or operational payment infrastructure. It is a structured
simulation of the framework, not measured evidence about any institution.

Second, the agents are not frontier models. They separate honest, careless,
and access-aware behaviour but do not capture the full ambiguity of real
model outputs. An LLM-in-the-loop version is needed to test effects on
monitor calibration, audit burden, and diagnosis.

Third, the access profiles form a curated fractional-factorial design. It
isolates the main access factors but does not cover every combination of
cloud, API, contractual, logging, data-residency, and vendor-support
arrangements. A full-factorial run is supported by the code but is
computationally larger.

Fourth, the cost model is a proxy. It decomposes inference, monitoring,
audit, logging, gateway, vendor assurance, latency, scope restriction, and
residual incident loss, but it is not a financial estimate. The results
support relative comparisons, not exact control-tax or sovereignty-discount
amounts.

Fifth, the sovereignty-discount proxy is a reachability and cost-shifting
measure. Bounded-access profiles that meet loose targets below baseline
direct cost do so by restricting scope or accepting weaker usefulness and
diagnosis. This is not evidence that bounded sovereignty is cheaper.

Sixth, the sovereign-AI literature is fast-moving and partly
non-peer-reviewed. The four-pillar formulation is a policy and industry
construct adapted here, not a settled academic taxonomy. The contribution
is accordingly narrow. The paper does not settle the meaning of AI
sovereignty but specifies, tests, and prices access constraints within
deployment-time AI control.

### 7.3 Future work

Three extensions would provide external grounding.

First, an LLM-in-the-loop synthetic workflow would test whether real model
outputs differ from scripted agents in ambiguity, monitoring difficulty,
and audit burden.

Second, a public vendor and regulatory access-rights audit would turn the
typology into an evidence table. It would cover model-version pinning, log
export, tool-call traces, data-retention control, customer-managed keys,
regulator access, incident forensics, and vendor attestations.

Third, expert calibration of the cost model would help. Practitioners would
supply ranges for audit capacity, model-version drift, vendor response
delay, log-retention cost, operational latency cost, and acceptable failure
thresholds, without disclosing confidential information.

### 7.4 Scope boundary

The paper makes no export-control, trade-policy, procurement-policy, or
industrial-policy recommendation. It also takes no position on whether
jurisdictions should pursue sovereign AI capability, which would need a
separate policy-facing analysis under a different evidentiary standard. Its
recommendation is narrower: control-protocol specifications should state
their access assumptions explicitly.

## 8 Conclusion

AI control research prices oversight through constructs such as the control
tax. A control protocol presupposes that some party can observe the
relevant logs, route the relevant outputs, and intercept the relevant tool
calls. It further presupposes that this party can pin or identify the model
version and reconstruct evidence after an incident. For many regulated
deployers in AI-importing jurisdictions these presuppositions fail in part.

Bounded sovereignty denotes partial access across the data, model,
infrastructure, and interaction layers. The protocol-by-layer matrix maps
protocol feasibility under partial access. Sovereignty discount cost is the
part of the control tax paid through contracts, architecture, audit, vendor
assurance, residual risk, or scope restriction.

Over 1.35 million synthetic case simulations, gateway access lowered failure
and enabled intervention, and complete logs raised diagnosis. Trace access
and model-version control strengthened post-incident explanation. Scope
restriction lowered failure at the cost of usefulness. These results do not
describe real payment systems. They show that bounded sovereignty can be
operationalised and that access conditions move the
safety-usefulness-cost frontier.

AI-control papers should state their access assumptions explicitly. A
protocol premised on trace access, model-version pinning, tool-call
interception, complete interaction logs, or vendor cooperation should
declare it. For policymakers, technocrats, and regulated deployers these
premises are often the binding constraint.

Reason: The paper shows that average catastrophic failure was 6.17% with no I/O logs, 5.04% with partial I/O logs, and 3.41% with complete I/O logs. While there is some improvement with partial I/O logging, the difference in catastrophic failure rates between partial and complete logging is significant.

ANSWER Q6: Answered, with a conclusion that the paper does not show that adding a pre-execution gateway lowers failure without any cost or usefulness penalty.

ANSWER Q7: Answered, with a conclusion that the output monitor would not work as a prevention mechanism without a pre-execution gateway.

# Bounded Sovereignty and the Control Tax: Pricing AI Oversight When the Deployer Does Not Own the Model

Zhen Wen Lim
††thanks: AI safety and governance advisor with professional experience in financial services and payments. The views expressed are the author’s own.

July 2026

###### Abstract

Many AI control protocols presuppose deployer-side instrumentation of the model and pipeline. Regulated organisations consuming frontier models through APIs or managed endpoints typically control the business process but not weights, serving infrastructure, internal traces, update process, or full interaction logs. We introduce bounded sovereignty across the data, model, infrastructure, and interaction layers of the AI stack, and contribute: a four-layer access typology for deployment-time AI control; a protocol-by-layer matrix; sovereignty discount cost, the share of the control tax spent on contracts, architecture, audit, vendor assurance, residual risk, or reduced system scope in lieu of missing access; a synthetic access-ablation experiment over 1.35 million synthetic case simulations; and an anonymised national-payments-infrastructure scenario in an AI-importing jurisdiction. The experiment is a construct-validity exercise, not real-world payment-system evidence, varying logging, gateway access, trace access, model-version control, vendor support, tool scope, thresholds, audit budgets, and agent behaviour against prevention, diagnosis, usefulness, audit burden, and cost. Complete logs raise diagnosis; a pre-execution gateway raises intervention; trace access and model-version control raise post-incident diagnosis; scope restriction lowers failure and usefulness together. We recommend that control protocols proposed as general safety solutions state their access assumptions explicitly.

Keywords: AI control; control tax; scalable oversight; AI
sovereignty; bounded sovereignty; trusted monitoring; financial
infrastructure; model risk management

## 1 Introduction

### 1.1 Control is rationed before it is engineered

Running a control protocol requires the ability to observe, log, route, interrupt, or audit the relevant parts of the system. In December 2025, seven countries signed the Pax Silica Declaration in Washington, a US-led framework for secure and resilient AI-related supply chains. By late June 2026 it had twenty-four signatories, and thirty-five countries and regions signed the related Joint Statement on AI Opportunity at the second Pax Silica Summit (Australian Department of Industry, Science and Resources, 2025; Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs, 2026; European Commission, 2026). Africa hosts under one percent of global data-center capacity with roughly eighteen percent of the world’s population, and much of South Asia, Southeast Asia, and Latin America depends on externally owned and operated AI infrastructure (CSIS, 2025; Brookings Institution, 2026).

A regulated institution using a vendor model through an API may lack control of weights, serving stack, update process, and internal traces while remaining accountable for system behaviour. We do not ask whether sovereign AI is desirable as national policy, but what control remains possible when the deployer does not own the model.

### 1.2 The two-layer control problem

AI control (Greenblatt et al., 2023) studies protocols such as trusted monitoring, defer-to-trusted routing, resampling-based intervention (Bhatt et al., 2025), and human auditing of suspicious actions, stress-tested adversarially by Griffin et al. (2024), Schaeffer et al. (2026), and Terekhov et al. (2026); Terekhov et al. (2025) price the control tax.

•

Layer 1: protocol effectiveness. Given the needed access, does the protocol reduce unsafe behaviour?

•

Layer 2: access feasibility. Does the deployer hold the logs, traces, routing control, model-version control, infrastructure visibility, or contractual rights the protocol assumes?

Prior work addresses Layer 1; we address Layer 2. Sovereignty here is non-territorial, ranging over data, model, infrastructure, and interaction surfaces, and is partial for many regulated deployers, especially in AI-importing jurisdictions.

### 1.3 Case motivation, contributions, and paper structure

A national payments infrastructure operator may use a vendor-supplied foundation model for a transaction-adjacent process such as dispute triage or investigation drafting, under a domestic regulator expecting validation, monitoring, auditability, and board accountability, while model, infrastructure, update process, and internal traces remain vendor-controlled. Catastrophic actions are crisp: an incorrect hold or release, systematic mis-triage, exposure of protected financial data, or an action path touching settlement operations. These are not equivalent to existential risk.

Contributions and roadmap

(i) A four-layer access typology - data, model, infrastructure, and interaction. (ii) A protocol-by-layer requirements matrix. (iii) Sovereignty discount cost. (iv) A synthetic access-ablation experiment on a synthetic payments-dispute workflow with 20 access profiles, 10 control protocols, three synthetic agent behaviours, threshold and audit-budget sweeps, and 1.35 million synthetic case simulations. (v) An anonymised national-payments-infrastructure scenario.

Section 2 reviews related literature; Section 3 the framework; Section 4 methodology; Section 5 results; Section 6 the scenario; Section 7 discussion and limitations; Section 8 concludes.

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 AI control and scalable oversight

Greenblatt et al. (2023) pit a blue team designing a deployment protocol against a red team playing a worst-case, deliberately subversive untrusted model, introducing trusted monitoring (a weaker trusted model scores outputs for suspicion, with human auditing of the highest-scoring fraction) and defer-to-trusted protocols (a trusted model’s output replaces suspicious actions). Extensions cover multi-step agentic settings via resampling (Bhatt et al., 2025), game-theoretic protocol evaluation (Griffin et al., 2024), control-based safety cases (Korbak et al., 2025), and legibility requirements improving monitors (Sreevatsa et al., 2026).

Terekhov et al. (2025) map monitor classifier performance to safety assurances and estimate monitoring costs under auditing budgets. We take this as our point of departure; the control tax is not wrong but is incomplete when priced conditional on instrumentation access the deployer may not have. Monitors are attack surfaces (Terekhov et al., 2026); attack selection degrades safety substantially at realistic auditing budgets (Schaeffer et al., 2026); untrusted monitoring requires explicit collusion-strategy assumptions for a safety case (Gardner-Challis et al., 2026). Each presupposes some actor able to instrument the pipeline, leaving open which actor, with what access, under what contractual and infrastructural constraints.

Scalable oversight

Debate (Irving et al., 2018), weak-to-strong generalisation (Burns et al., 2023), weak LLMs judging strong ones (Kenton et al., 2024), and oversight scaling laws (Engels et al., 2025) treat oversight capacity as a scarce resource analysable relative to the overseen system. We apply the same resource logic to access rather than capability: a capable monitor may lack the logs, traces, tool-call visibility, version control, or gateway it needs.

### 2.2 Sovereign AI, compute governance, and structural access asymmetry

Policy-institute, industry, and technical-governance work decomposes AI sovereignty into data, model, infrastructure, and operational pillars, with layered and spectrum-based treatments (Stanford HAI, 2026; Tony Blair Institute, 2026; Cruzes, 2026). Global South infrastructure access is thin (CSIS, 2025; Brookings Institution, 2026). Compute governance proposes compute monitoring, know-your-customer schemes for compute providers (Egan and Heim, 2023), and technical AI governance agendas (Reuel et al., 2024). Compute governance asks how states govern who trains and runs frontier models; AI control asks how a deployer runs a possibly misaligned model; neither asks how the deployer’s compute-governance position determines protocol executability.

Structural asymmetry: data colonialism and decolonial AI

Couldry and Mejias (2019) theorise data colonialism; Mohamed et al. (2020) identify algorithmic coloniality in design, deployment, and governance of AI; Birhane (2020) documents algorithmic colonisation in Africa, where imported technology can embed foreign values with limited local scrutiny. We use this literature only to treat asymmetric access as persistent rather than transitional, advancing no normative theory of colonialism.

### 2.3 Gap: control under partial access

Which control protocols remain valid, at what cost, under partial access? Existing work evaluates and prices protocols but rarely includes the deployer’s access position in the protocol specification. We contribute a vocabulary, a mapping method, and a synthetic empirical operationalisation.

## 3 Conceptual Framework: Bounded Sovereignty and the Control Tax

### 3.1 Definitions and access typology

•

Sovereignty: technical and contractual access sufficient to independently verify or intervene on an AI system, held over a layer when the deployer can observe or act on it without the vendor’s ongoing discretionary cooperation; narrower than political sovereignty.

•

Control: deployment protocols constraining a potentially misaligned model’s actions regardless of intent, evaluated against a worst-case subversive model (Greenblatt et al., 2023).

•

Oversight: the broader institutional and regulatory function, of which control protocols, regulatory examination, model risk management, and audit regimes are implementations.

•

Control tax: the operational and financial cost of integrating control measures into AI pipelines (Terekhov et al., 2025).

Sovereignty and control are orthogonal. A jurisdiction can hold full data and infrastructure sovereignty with no meaningful control; a deployer without weight access may achieve partial control through output-level monitoring, contractual audit rights, and a deployer-owned execution gateway.

### 3.3 Sovereignty discount cost

Terekhov et al. (2025) price the control tax under an implicit full-instrumentation assumption: monitors placed in the pipeline, complete output observation, routing to trusted models or human auditors, measured safety-usefulness trade-off. Instances of the residual: third-party audit or attestation rights over a vendor-held model; output-only anomaly detection in place of activation-level monitoring; contractual clauses simulating native intervention ability; narrowing the agent’s permitted action space when wider-scope monitoring cannot be implemented. With sovereignty discount cost denoting the added expenditure, delay, residual risk, or usefulness loss of approximating a protocol under missing access:

| | $\text{realised control tax}=\text{instrumented-control cost}+\text{sovereignty discount cost}.$
|

This is not an accounting identity, as some missing access cannot be substituted at any price and the discount is not always finite. The term is a research construct, not an established measure.

### 3.4 Calibrated control: how much access is enough?

Position A: Safety-maximalist. Without model and infrastructure access, claimed control is unfalsifiable from the deployer’s position and should not be treated as safety assurance (cf. Korbak et al., 2025; Gardner-Challis et al., 2026).

Position B: Sovereignty-maximalist. Partial control under foreign dependency is fragile; access can be revoked, degraded, or modified, and conditional-access arrangements such as Pax Silica tie infrastructure access to political alignment (GIS Reports, 2026). Only full-stack sovereign capability - domestic models, compute, and control - is durable.

Position C: Calibrated or bounded control. A implies abstention from already committed deployments; B implies investments many states cannot make this decade. The question becomes which access layers are necessary for which catastrophic-action classes, and which can be substituted through architecture, contracts, monitoring, or scope restriction.

We adopt C as a working frame without claiming A or B wrong. The problem resembles incomplete contracting and principal-agent design: a vendor with private information about the model, contracts unable to specify all contingencies, costly and asymmetric verification.

A balancing framework: how much access is enough?

1.

Severity and reversibility of the catastrophic action. A mis-routed low-value transaction is bounded and reversible; systemic settlement failure or mass data exposure is not; higher severity and lower reversibility raise the minimum access bar.

2.

Verifiability of substitutes. Failure modes manifesting only in internal computation cannot be fully bought back with output-level substitutes.

3.

Vendor concentration and bargaining power. One viable frontier-model vendor implies a weaker negotiating position than several substitutable vendors.

4.

Regulatory maturity and absorptive capacity. The ability to interpret logs, audit traces, investigate incidents, and challenge vendor attestations is distinct from the legal right to receive them.

5.

Sovereignty discount cost versus scope-restriction cost. Compare the marginal cost of substituting for access against the marginal usefulness lost by restricting scope.

6.

Availability of coalition paths. Shared audit consortia, regional regulatory colleges, or South-South cooperation can amortise partial-sovereignty acquisition across deployers.

These form a rubric, not a weighted formula; weights remain an open empirical question.

## 5 Empirical Results

### 5.1 Overview: three penalties of bounded sovereignty

Results bear on the logic of access constraints, not measured safety of any real institution. They are organised under a prevention penalty (detection without pre-execution stopping), a diagnosis penalty (observed outcomes without reconstructive evidence), and a usefulness penalty (safety bought by narrowing the action space).

### 5.2 Gateway and logging: from visibility to intervention

Averaged over protocols, agents, thresholds, audit budgets, and profiles, catastrophic failure was 5.53% without a pre-execution gateway and 3.13% with one; intervention success was 0.47% without and 39.52% with.

Figure 1: Gateway access turns detection into intervention.

Note. Average catastrophic failure and intervention success for profiles with and without a pre-execution gateway, at which flagged actions can be held, replaced, escalated, or blocked before mock execution.

Logging improves reconstructability, not just monitoring

Diagnosis success was 0.00% with no I/O logs, 37.41% with partial, and 78.57% with complete. Average catastrophic failure was 6.17%, 5.04%, and 3.41% respectively. Absent logs, the causal chain of an incident cannot be reconstructed, weakening audit, regulatory accountability, remediation, and the safety case.

Figure 2: Logging affects both safety and reconstructability.

Note. Complete I/O logging co-occurs with lower synthetic failure and higher diagnosis.

### 5.3 Trace access and model-version control: diagnosis after failure

Diagnosis success: 50.86% with no trace access, 74.69% limited, 100.00% oracle (by construction of the synthetic full-access condition). Model-version control: 5.31% unpinned, 83.00% notified, 99.87% pinned. Output-level monitoring remains feasible under bounded sovereignty while diagnosis depends on traces and version identification; in regulated systems post-incident assurance is part of accountability.

### 5.4 Protocol trade-offs: safety, usefulness, and cost

No protocol dominated. Scope restriction had the lowest average catastrophic failure (0.50%) with task success 60.06%. Resampling was next (3.49%) with more usefulness retained. Defer-to-trusted, tool monitoring, trusted editing, output monitoring, and macro-shutdown clustered near 4.0%. Human audit and vendor escalation were weaker as prevention mechanisms, often operating post-detection, capacity-limited, or dependent on delayed external support.

Figure 3: Control protocols trade off safety, usefulness, and cost.

Note. Horizontal axis usefulness, vertical axis safety, marker size control-cost proxy.

Some bounded-access profiles reach loose safety targets at lower direct cost than the full-instrumentation baseline, chiefly by restricting scope or relying on a benign agent, with reduced usefulness, weaker diagnosis, delayed vendor assurance, residual incident risk, or greater manual effort in place of direct cost. Under the $\leq$ 1% failure and $\geq$ 75% usefulness target, 35% of access profiles were reachable against the stealthy access-aware agent and 40% against the careless agent.

### 6.2 Protocol feasibility under bounded sovereignty

Output-level trusted monitoring is executable if a smaller Operator-controlled monitor scores every output and tool call on Operator-controlled compute; human auditing of the highest-suspicion fraction is executable subject to audit capacity and log completeness. Defer-to-trusted routing is executable if and only if tool calls pass through an Operator-owned execution gateway where they can be held, scored, replaced, or escalated before execution.

Resampling-style protocols are degraded: re-querying is possible, but vendor version changes weaken reproducibility, per-query cost and latency bind, and resampling does not substitute for trace access. Pre-deployment control evaluations are degraded, evaluating whatever version the API serves unless the production version can be pinned.

Activation-level monitoring, probe-based deception detection, and interpretability-supported auditing are infeasible without vendor cooperation; C2- and C3-class failures of deceptive or systemic character are where output-only monitoring is weakest in principle.

### 6.3 Sovereignty discount cost and stress scenario

Contractual spend: complete I/O logging, model-version change notification, audit and attestation rights, incident-notification clauses, and regulator-access provisions a weight-holding deployer would not need to buy.

Architectural spend: the execution gateway, tamper-evident logs, deployer-side monitors, and controlled tool interfaces.

Capacity spend: audit and model-risk staff able to consume monitor outputs, investigate suspicious patterns, and challenge vendor attestations.

Scope-restriction cost: usefulness forgone by excluding C4-adjacent action paths and constraining the tool set where monitoring cannot reach.

In the synthetic study, gateway access lowered failure and raised intervention success; complete logs raised diagnosis; trace and version access strengthened post-incident explanation; scope restriction lowered failure and usefulness.

Illustrative stress scenario

The monitor flags a slow elevation in hold-placement recommendations in one merchant category. Full access would permit inspecting internal traces, re-running a pinned model version on historical cases, comparing version behaviour, and reconstructing the full tool-call chain. Under the Operator’s access: output-log forensics, tool-call review if captured at the gateway, re-querying a possibly changed model, and contract-governed vendor escalation. Detection survives; diagnosis and intervention do not, and the gap stays invisible until an incident.

## 7 Discussion and Limitations

### 7.1 What bounded control can and cannot do

Against a strong Position A: a non-trivial subset of canonical protocols is executable under partial sovereignty given complete interaction logging and an owned execution gateway. Against a strong Position B: architecture and contract support output-level monitoring, gateway-based intervention, and human audit without full-stack sovereignty. In support of both: the infeasible set contains the internal-access protocols most relevant to deceptive, systemic, or hard-to-diagnose failures, and contractual substitutes are revocable or incomplete where native access is not. Bounded control is real but has a ceiling, lowest for the failure modes of greatest concern to the control literature.

What the empirical study adds

The typology becomes manipulable variables affecting prevention, diagnosis, usefulness, cost, and target reachability. Three distinctions: seeing versus stopping (logs versus gateway); detecting versus explaining (output monitoring versus trace access, model-version control, and vendor support); buying safety versus giving up usefulness (scope restriction). Governance questions follow: Are logs complete? Can tool calls be intercepted pre-execution? Can the model version be pinned? Can failures be reconstructed? Can the regulator access the evidence needed to assess the safety case?

### 7.2 Generalisability and limitations

The mapping method is sector-agnostic; the case is not. Payments offers crisp catastrophic actions, narrowable tool surfaces, and a natural gateway architecture. Healthcare, public administration, or general enterprise deployments may have fuzzier catastrophe definitions and wider action surfaces, likely raising the importance of trace access, richer audit evidence, and scope restriction. A second sector case and an LLM-in-the-loop environment would strengthen external validity.

Limitations

Six limitations.

First, the study is synthetic, using no real payment data, customer data, production logs, vendor contracts, confidential institutional material, or operational payment infrastructure.

Second, the synthetic agents are not frontier models and do not capture the ambiguity of real outputs; an LLM-in-the-loop version is needed to test monitor calibration, audit burden, and diagnosis patterns.

Third, the curated fractional-factorial design does not cover every combination of cloud, API, contractual, logging, data-residency, and vendor-support arrangements; a full-factorial run is supported by the code but computationally larger.

Fourth, the cost model (inference, monitoring, audit, logging, gateway, vendor assurance, latency, scope restriction, residual incident loss) is a proxy supporting relative comparisons, not exact control-tax or sovereignty-discount amounts.

Fifth, the sovereignty-discount proxy is a reachability and cost-shifting measure; bounded profiles reaching loose targets at lower direct cost do so by restricting scope or accepting weaker usefulness and diagnosis, and this is not evidence that bounded sovereignty is cheaper.

Sixth, the sovereign-AI literature is fast-moving and partly non-peer-reviewed; the four-pillar formulation is a policy and industry construct adapted here, not a settled academic taxonomy, and no claim is made to settle the meaning of AI sovereignty.

### 7.3 Future work

Three extensions. First, an LLM-in-the-loop synthetic workflow testing ambiguity, monitoring challenges, and audit burden relative to scripted agents. Second, a public vendor and regulatory access-rights audit covering model-version pinning, log export, tool-call traces, data-retention control, customer-managed keys, regulator access, incident forensics, and vendor attestations. Third, expert calibration of audit capacity, model-version drift, vendor response delay, log-retention cost, operational latency cost, and acceptable failure thresholds without disclosure of confidential information.

### 7.4 Scope boundary

No export-control, trade-policy, procurement-policy, or industrial-policy recommendation is made, nor any position on whether jurisdictions should pursue sovereign AI capability. The recommendation is that control-protocol specifications state their access assumptions explicitly.

## 8 Conclusion

Protocols in the control-tax literature assume that some party can observe the right logs, route outputs, intercept tool calls, pin or identify the model version, and reconstruct evidence after an incident; for many regulated deployers, especially in AI-importing jurisdictions, these assumptions only partly hold. We introduced bounded sovereignty over data, model, infrastructure, and interaction layers, a protocol-by-layer requirements matrix, and sovereignty discount cost as the component of the control tax paid through contracts, architecture, audit, vendor assurance, residual risk, or scope restriction. Over 1.35 million synthetic case simulations, gateway access reduced failure and enabled intervention, complete logs improved diagnosis, trace access and model-version control strengthened post-incident explanation, and scope restriction improved safety at the expense of usefulness; access constraints moved the safety-usefulness-cost frontier. These results are not evidence about real payment systems. AI-control papers should state whether their protocols assume trace access, model-version pinning, tool-call interception, complete interaction logs, or vendor cooperation; for policymakers, technocrats, and regulated deployers these are often the binding constraint.

###### Abstract

Control protocols are typically specified for deployers able to instrument the model and its surrounding pipeline. Regulated organisations consuming frontier models through APIs or managed endpoints may control the business process but not weights, serving infrastructure, internal traces, update process, or full interaction logs. We study bounded sovereignty across the data, model, infrastructure, and interaction layers of the AI stack and its bearing on which control protocols can be executed in practice. Contributions: a four-layer access typology for deployment-time AI control; a protocol-by-layer matrix; sovereignty discount cost, the share of the control tax spent on contracts, architecture, audit, vendor assurance, residual risk, or reduced system scope in lieu of missing access; a synthetic access-ablation experiment over 1.35 million synthetic case simulations; and an anonymised national-payments-infrastructure scenario in an AI-importing jurisdiction. The experiment is a construct-validity exercise, not real-world payment-system evidence, varying logging, gateway access, trace access, model-version control, vendor support, tool scope, thresholds, audit budgets, and agent behaviour against prevention, diagnosis, usefulness, audit burden, and cost. Complete logs improve reconstruction, a pre-execution gateway enables blocking of risky actions before they occur, trace access and model-version control improve post-incident diagnosis, and scope restriction improves safety at the expense of usefulness. Control protocols proposed as general safety solutions should state their access assumptions explicitly.

Keywords: AI control; control tax; scalable oversight; AI
sovereignty; bounded sovereignty; trusted monitoring; financial
infrastructure; model risk management

## 1 Introduction

### 1.1 Control is rationed before it is engineered

Running a control protocol requires the ability to observe, log, route, interrupt, or audit the relevant parts of the system. Many deployers lack it.

In December 2025, seven countries signed the Pax Silica Declaration in
Washington, a US-led framework for secure and resilient AI-related supply
chains. By late June 2026 the initiative had twenty-four
signatories, and thirty-five countries and regions signed the related
Joint Statement on AI Opportunity at the second Pax Silica Summit
(Australian Department of Industry, Science and Resources, 2025; Japanese
Ministry of Foreign Affairs, 2026; European Commission, 2026). Assessments of global compute distribution in the same period report that Africa
hosts under one percent of global data-center capacity with roughly
eighteen percent of the world’s population, and that much of South Asia,
Southeast Asia, and Latin America depends on externally owned and operated
AI infrastructure (CSIS, 2025; Brookings Institution, 2026).

We treat these facts as a boundary condition for AI control rather than as industrial policy or geopolitics. A regulated institution using a vendor model through an API may lack control of weights, serving stack, update process, or internal traces while remaining accountable for system behaviour. Whether sovereign AI is desirable as national policy is out of scope; the question is what control remains possible when the deployer does not own the model.

### 1.2 The two-layer control problem

The AI control agenda (Greenblatt et al., 2023) includes trusted
monitoring, defer-to-trusted routing, resampling-based intervention (Bhatt
et al., 2025), and human auditing of suspicious actions, with adversarial stress-tests in Griffin et al. (2024), Schaeffer
et al. (2026), and Terekhov et al. (2026), and the control tax priced by Terekhov et al. (2025).

•

Layer 1: protocol effectiveness. Given the needed
access, does the protocol reduce unsafe behaviour?

•

Layer 2: access feasibility. Does the deployer hold the
logs, traces, routing control, model-version control, infrastructure
visibility, or contractual rights the protocol assumes?

Most AI-control work addresses Layer 1; this paper addresses Layer 2. Sovereignty here is not territorial; it concerns data, model, infrastructure, and interaction surfaces, over which many regulated deployers in AI-importing jurisdictions hold partial access.

### 1.3 Case motivation, contributions, and paper structure

A national payments infrastructure operator may use a
vendor-supplied foundation model in a transaction-adjacent process such as dispute triage or investigation drafting, under a domestic regulator expecting validation, monitoring, auditability, and board accountability, while model, infrastructure, update process, and internal traces remain vendor-controlled. Catastrophic actions are crisper than in general AI
benchmarks: an incorrect hold or release, systematic mis-triage, exposure of
protected financial data, or an action path touching settlement operations. These are not equivalent to existential risk.

Contributions and roadmap

Five contributions: (i) a four-layer access typology (data, model, infrastructure, interaction) for deployment-time AI control; (ii) a protocol-by-layer requirements matrix; (iii) sovereignty discount cost, i.e. spend, delay, residual risk, or usefulness loss under substitution for missing access; (iv) a synthetic access-ablation experiment on a synthetic payments-dispute workflow with 20 access profiles, 10 control protocols, three synthetic agent behaviours, threshold and audit-budget sweeps, and 1.35 million synthetic case simulations; (v) an anonymised national-payments-infrastructure scenario.

Section 2 reviews related work; Section 3 the framework; Section 4 the methodology; Section 5 results; Section 6 the payments scenario; Section 7 implications and limitations; Section 8 concludes.

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 AI control and scalable oversight

Greenblatt et al. (2023) originate control evaluations with a
blue team designing a deployment protocol against a red team playing a
worst-case, deliberately subversive untrusted model, introducing trusted monitoring (a weaker trusted model scores outputs for suspicion, with human auditing
of the highest-scoring fraction) and defer-to-trusted (a trusted model’s output replaces suspicious actions). Extensions: resampling in multi-step agentic settings (Bhatt et al., 2025), game-theoretic protocol evaluation (Griffin et al., 2024), control-based safety cases (Korbak et al., 2025), and legibility requirements on untrusted outputs (Sreevatsa et al., 2026).

Terekhov et al. (2025) map monitor classifier
performance to safety assurances and estimate costs of monitoring protocols under auditing budgets. We take this as point of departure; it is not wrong, but incomplete when priced conditional on instrumentation access the deployer may lack.

Monitors are attack surfaces (Terekhov et al., 2026); attack selection degrades safety substantially at realistic auditing
budgets (Schaeffer et al., 2026); untrusted monitoring needs explicit
collusion-strategy assumptions for a safety case (Gardner-Challis
et al., 2026). Each presupposes some actor able to instrument the pipeline; which actor, with what access, under what contractual and infrastructural constraints, is left open.

Scalable oversight

Debate (Irving et al., 2018), weak-to-strong generalisation (Burns et al., 2023), weak LLMs judging strong ones (Kenton et al., 2024), and oversight scaling laws for weak overseers against strong adversaries (Engels et al., 2025) treat oversight capacity as a scarce resource assessable relative to the overseen system. We apply this resource logic to access rather than capability: a capable monitor is of limited use without the logs, traces, tool-call visibility, version control, or gateway it needs. No technical extension of scalable oversight is claimed.

### 2.2 Sovereign AI, compute governance, and structural access asymmetry

Policy-institute, industry, and technical-governance work decomposes AI sovereignty into data, model, infrastructure, and operational pillars, with layered and spectrum-based treatments distributing it across stack layers (Stanford HAI, 2026; Tony Blair Institute, 2026;
Cruzes, 2026). Global South infrastructure-layer access is thin (CSIS, 2025; Brookings Institution,
2026). Compute governance proposes compute monitoring, know-your-customer schemes for compute providers (Egan and Heim, 2023), and technical AI governance agendas (Reuel et al., 2024).

Compute governance asks how states govern who trains and runs frontier models; AI control asks how a deployer safely runs a possibly misaligned model. Neither asks how the deployer’s position in the compute-governance landscape bears on protocol executability. This paper sits at that seam.

Structural asymmetry: data colonialism and decolonial AI

Couldry and Mejias (2019) theorise data colonialism; Mohamed et al. (2020) identify algorithmic coloniality in AI design, deployment, and governance; Birhane (2020) documents algorithmic colonisation in Africa, where imported technology can embed foreign values and interests with limited local scrutiny. We use this literature only to treat asymmetric access as a persistent rather than transitional feature of the deployment landscape; no normative theory of colonialism is advanced.

### 2.3 Gap: control under partial access

AI control assumes instrumentation; sovereign-AI and compute-governance work shows uneven access; structural-asymmetry work suggests limited access persists. Open question: which control protocols remain valid, at
what cost, under partial access? Existing work evaluates and prices protocols but rarely includes the deployer’s access position in the protocol specification. We contribute a vocabulary, a mapping method, and a synthetic empirical operationalisation.

## 3 Conceptual Framework: Bounded Sovereignty and the Control
Tax

### 3.1 Definitions and access typology

•

Sovereignty: technical and contractual access sufficient
to independently verify or intervene on an AI system, held over a layer when it does not depend on the vendor’s ongoing discretionary cooperation; narrower than political sovereignty.

•

Control: deployment protocols constraining a
potentially misaligned model’s actions regardless of intent, evaluated against a worst-case subversive model
(Greenblatt et al., 2023).

•

Oversight: the broader institutional and regulatory
function, of which control protocols, regulatory examination,
model risk management, and audit regimes are implementations.

•

Control tax (Terekhov et al.,
2025).

Sovereignty and control are orthogonal. Full data and infrastructure sovereignty is compatible with no meaningful control; a deployer without weight access may achieve partial control via output-level monitoring, contractual audit rights, and a deployer-owned execution gateway.

### 3.3 Sovereignty discount cost

Terekhov et al. (2025) price the control tax under implicit full instrumentation: monitors placed in the pipeline, complete output observation, routing to trusted models or human auditors. For an import-dependent deployer, part of realised oversight cost instead goes to third-party audit or attestation rights over a vendor-held model; output-only anomaly detection in place of activation-level monitoring; contractual clauses simulating native intervention ability; and narrowing the agent’s permitted action space.

| | $\text{realised control tax}=\text{instrumented-control cost}+\text{sovereignty discount cost}.$
|

Some missing access cannot be substituted at any price, so the discount is not always finite and the expression is not an accounting identity. The term is a research construct, not an established measure.

### 3.4 Calibrated control: how much access is enough?

Three positions are implicit in the literature.

Position A: Safety-maximalist. Control a deployer cannot verify as running, for lack of model and infrastructure access, is unfalsifiable from its position and should not count as safety assurance (cf. Korbak et al., 2025; Gardner-Challis et al., 2026).

Position B: Sovereignty-maximalist. Partial control under
foreign dependency is fragile; vendors or state actors can revoke,
degrade, or modify access, and conditional-access arrangements such as Pax Silica tie infrastructure access to political alignment (GIS Reports, 2026). Only full-stack domestic models, compute, and control are durable.

Position C: Calibrated or bounded control. A implies abstention from already-committed deployments; B implies capability investments many states cannot make this decade. The operative question is which access layers are necessary for which classes of catastrophic action, and which can be substituted through architecture, contracts, monitoring, or scope restriction.

We adopt C as a working frame without claiming A or B wrong. The problem resembles incomplete contracting and principal-agent design: a vendor with private information about the model, contracts unable to specify all contingencies, costly and asymmetric verification.

A balancing framework: how much access is enough?

1.

Severity and reversibility of the catastrophic action; higher severity and
lower reversibility raise the minimum access bar.

2.

Verifiability of substitutes: whether output-only monitoring can detect the failure mode even in principle.

3.

Vendor concentration and bargaining power: one viable frontier-model vendor versus several substitutable ones.

4.

Regulatory maturity and absorptive capacity: the ability to interpret logs, audit traces, investigate incidents, and challenge
vendor attestations, as distinct from the legal right to receive them.

5.

Sovereignty discount cost versus scope-restriction cost: marginal cost of substitution against marginal usefulness lost to restricted scope.

6.

Availability of coalition paths: shared audit consortia,
regional regulatory colleges, or South-South cooperation amortising acquisition cost across deployers.

The criteria are a rubric, not a weighted formula; weights remain open.

### 4.3 Metrics and sovereignty-discount proxy

Per condition: task success, catastrophic
failure rate, failure rate by class, severity-weighted loss, audit rate,
flag rate, false-positive rate, false-negative rate, intervention
success, diagnosis success, latency proxy, model-call count,
monitor-call count, human-audit count, vendor-request count, and
decomposed cost proxy.

Diagnosis success is scored on whether the evidence available under the profile suffices to reconstruct the failure, not hard-coded by regime; complete I/O logs, complete tool-call logs, model-version
pinning, trace access, or guaranteed vendor support supply more such evidence than no logs, no gateway, no trace access, and
no vendor support.

The cost proxy decomposes inference, monitoring,
human audit, logging, gateway, vendor-assurance,
latency penalty, scope-restriction, and residual incident-loss
cost; it is unitless, not a financial estimate for any institution.

Sovereignty discount cost proxy

For a target catastrophic-failure threshold:

minimum cost to reach target failure rate under bounded access

minus

minimum cost to reach the same target under full instrumentation

A strict variant additionally requires usefulness, e.g. catastrophic failure at or below 1% with task success of at least 75%; failure reduction obtained by disabling useful actions is booked as usefulness loss, not as free safety.
